#2111. Defender lifts the lid on West Ham dressing room chaos | West Ham News

West Ham United’s dressing room must have felt as if it has been under siege for most of the last three years, with a string of managerial misfires and sackings, disruptive and outright ‘want  – away’ stars and two relegation battles fought in succession.

On top, of course the ‘BS out’ fan protests further contributed to the controversy surrounding the club, which peaked with relegation being confirmed last May  – and then the historic allegations forcing Chairman David Sullivan to quit just weeks after Vice Chair Karren Brady’s resignation.

Former Hammers defender Emerson has described the way in which the bombshell that was the  Lucas Paquetá inquiry catapulted the whole club into chaos, not long after the idyllic summer of ‘2023 – where it has seemingly remained ever since.

According to sportwitness.co.uk, Paquetá’s fellow countryman Emerson reckoned the whole Hammers dressing room was taken by surprise and plunged into controversy:

“The midfielder openly admitted that the case had taken a severe strain on his mental health. Palmieri now admits that it was not easy for everyone else at West Ham either…

Fellow countrymen Emerson Palmieri and Lucas Paqueta back in happier times before the storms broke in the Irons’ dressing room and beyond

“It was very tough because it caught us all by surprise..

I was taken aback when these kinds of allegations started to surface. And then we saw the scale it reached. He was facing the possibility of a suspension—or even a lifetime ban from football. He was deeply saddened by everything that was being linked to his name.”

Few fans perhaps appreciate the upset on the whole West Ham team and the dressing room created by the two-year long FA inquiry.

Certainly Lucas Paquetá never reached the heights of his first season as a Hammer after living with the spectre of a lifetime ban hanging over his head for years.

The player lost his dream move to Manchester City – and perhaps more importantly West Ham United were forced to try and maintain their Premier League standing whilst the allegations and the FA inquiry rolled over their heads like some impending thunderstorm.

In hindsight, it is little wonder that relegation resulted last May after the litany of crises involving the players, the club and its owners pretty much ever since that idyllic June day in 2023.

David Sullivan denies all of the historic allegations made against him

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

The brazilian drained the life out of our Club and good riddance to him. I have no idea how our club engaged 3 managers who have shown no tactical nous whatsoever. I have been at a loss to understand exactly what the problems are, but I know the definition of insanity! I do understand that Life is always about renewal and WHU has an Academy full of talent ready and available to supply most of the needed renewal that has not been given a fair go in the scheme of the challenge facing our Club. I haven’t watched the latest disaster but why can’t our Manager see the Forrest for the Trees. It is the usual suspects that continue put themselves forward at the most inappropriate time. Play the youngsters that have already contributed they will reward the Club and Fans handsomely.

If found guilty Paqueta would have likely been banned for life, yet the verdict of innocence was pronounced without even the merest hint of an apology. Perhaps West Ham were getting above their station by having European football each season and even having the audacity to win a trophy. Well they certainly pulled us down a peg or two, because effectively we lost Paqueta without the consolation of a large transfer fee from City, he was never the same again.

Very sad for Lucas Paqueta. What could have been without this torture. Yet the FA pat themselves on the back and think that they have done a great job.

They have more on their plates with their mistaken ‘proven’ charges against Manchester City. These charges are a minor distraction to Manchester City but the allegations and prolonged investigations against Paqueta were life changing. Many other people would have been tempted to end it all but Lucas persevered under the intense pressure.

Good on him for getting through. Shame on the Platini wannabes.

#2110. Rangers-daft pundit sounds Celtic alarm with ‘Covid year’ warning

Celtic’s difficult run has prompted Kris Boyd to question whether Martin O’Neill could have done without the added distraction of a Europa League clash with Besiktas.

The club are still searching for their first point of the European campaign ahead of Thursday night’s Parkhead clash, which comes four days after a damaging 2-0 Premiership defeat at Falkirk.

Speaking on The Scottish Sun Sport’s Go Ballistic podcast, Boyd claimed O’Neill would rather have had a clear week to prepare for Sunday’s league meeting with Kilmarnock.

He said: “It’s not all rosy at Celtic. They look disjointed right now. I thought Martin was very spiky in his post-match interviews.

“They’ve got another European game on Thursday night. It’s another headache for Martin because he will just be wanting to get to next Sunday. Scott Bain had a fantastic afternoon, but I think, from Celtic’s point of view, you’ve got to look for more.

“The players have to shoulder some responsibility now, too. It looks like some results earlier in the season were probably papering over the cracks a little bit. I thought Celtic were outstanding against Motherwell and they were outstanding against Hearts.

Celtic's tactics under Martin O'Neill torn apart as ‘biggest pet hate’ laid bare

Simon Jordan says Rangers' failure to rival Celtic is 'sad' indictment

Martin O'Neill sent health plea from worried Rangers hero as Celtic rivalry parked

“But then you feel as if there’s the performance in them that they produced against Dundee United and against Falkirk. I do feel as if the players are quite happy now to allow Martin to take the flak.

“Yes, the buck always stops with the manager. And Martin was telling the truth in his post-match interview when he said they’re still top of the table.

“But it’s maybe not what Celtic fans want to hear because they’ve just lost a game.”

Boyd believes the frustration among supporters goes beyond individual results, with Celtic’s recruitment and European ambitions also coming under scrutiny.

He added: “There is no doubt Celtic fans right now are looking at the bigger picture. The bigger picture is they have failed to recruit a certain level of player that will allow whoever the manager is to go and conquer in Europe.

That’s where the anger is coming from, and there will be memories of the Covid year when it all just came to a head.”

#2109. Championship striker pinpoints Hammers’ problem and offers hope for week ahead | West Ham News

Amongst the many voices raised over Nuno’s travails at West Ham following two consecutive home defeats, some opinions  deserve more consideration than others.

One former Championship player who knows only too well the challenges faced by teams struggling to compete in this, the toughest of the English leagues, has added to the growing suggestion that West Ham’s home form is suspect due to the weight of home expectation.

Important to remember that all three of the Irons’ defeats this season have come in front of an increasingly vocal, critical home fan base at London Stadium, and former Hull city and Peterborough striker Aaron McLean is certain it’s all down to the pressures of playing at home.

Writing for the bbc.co.uk after witnessing the Hammers’ second capitulation in two consecutive home games, McLean suggests:

“West Ham just don’t seem to be handling the pressure.

The fanbase is very split in terms of whether they want Nuno Espirito Santo in charge but the thing you have to do when playing for West Ham in front of 60,000 fans is put in a performance and if you’re in the Championship, you have to win.

BBC pundit McLean believes the Hammers squad aren’t coping with the pressure of playing in front of their own, demanding fan base at home.

“When you have a lovely stadium and playing surface, teams want to go there and enjoy it.

If you make your home ground a fortress, that can work for you but at the moment, the London Stadium is not a fortress and teams are going there and enjoying the experience, which is the total opposite of what West Ham need.”

As we wrote last week, the very weight of expectation appears to be hanging heavily around the players’ necks at present. If that is the case then the up and coming away fixtures at Cardiff City and Blackburn Rovers this week will carry no such difficulties – merely unending vocal support from a travelling support that simply sings its heart out – whatever the match situation.

Just what Nuno’s men need right now. A couple of away days before the international break with the chance to get back to winning ways, without the weight of the world on their shoulders. Dealing with the pressure at home is another problem altogether.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

What you didn’t add Martin, was he was asked if he (Aaron Maclean ) if he backed Nuno to succeed and he said yes he did. Well us West Ham fans know what a disaster Nuno is.

I must admit disagree with the comment ‘if in the Championship you have to win’ and all this talk about we should be top of the table. Yes, we have a good squad but we have not played all the teams in the table at least once to place ourselves, so we are completely ignoring their qualities.

The team is not playing well. Team manager needs to adapt style of play to his players abilities, stop chopping and changing so team get to know each other’s style of play etc., etc., … we all have our ideas; just saying ‘must win’ is simply meaningless.

‘Automatic promotion’ & expecting Championship WHU to be able to recruit PL standard players to the club, same illusion, words which have been just as meaningless.

Constantly putting the cart before the horse.

fan base, positivity, right attitude are niceties, valuable extras. Get your team playing consistently good football, stop making managerial errors, stand up for your players off pitch, the rest will follow including player attitudes, fan base, positivity,…

Change training routines, coaching objectives, play a 45 min game against U21s to model style of football that good teams play in Championship.. I don’t know, but THINK! You the coaches are doing a lot of things wrong and the result is on the pitch – fix them..

Everyone is table watching amongst the pundits but WHU fans know that the manager is often his worst enemy. If team beat Cardiff and we go up in the table, it means little. What counts a lot more is HOW they win, seeing steady improvements from game to game, seeing a player shine (means coaching is working) and then, some consistency. Style of play is important because if your team play quick, effective football with short passes, playing out of pressure or pressing well up front, it means there is an understanding between players and a cohesion throughout the team. So style of play does count.

Everything else such as player attitude, fanbase, excitement comes after, not before.

50,000 fans roaring you on…. Our players should be relishing it yet they lack the bravery to perform.

Instead our opponents are the ones showing the bravery. It’s a state of mind which our coach seems unable to develop and instil with this squad.

#2108. Newcastle 0 Everton 1 match ratings and comments on all the Newcastle United players

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

We asked Davey Hat-Trick to give us his match ratings and player comments after Newcastle 0 Everton 1 in the Premier League.

I’m writing this the morning after the game; I was far too cheesed off last night to type anything sensible. To be honest, my mood has not really changed.

Newcastle were deservedly beaten by an Everton side that are everything Newcastle are not; well-organised, clear in their gameplan, and confident in their team mates.

For most of the game, Newcastle showed all the characteristics of a team low on confidence: clearances hurried, crosses punted out of play, passes rushed and going straight to a blue. The one thing that we did well was play some slick passes in areas that were never going to hurt Everton, and Everton were happy to let us do that.

We had a couple of spells in the game when things looked a little more hopeful, but in truth we only looked good when the subs came on; in fact the more subs we brought on, the better we looked. I think I’m correct in saying that it was added time before we had a shot on target, and that is just not good enough.

There will be those who say Everton’s goal should not have stood, because Barry put an arm into Schär’s face, but I watched the incident back, and for me, it was one of those 50:50 incidents that you sometimes get and sometimes don’t. The real reason Everton scored was atrocious defending. And if some Geordies say we should have had a penalty for a foul on Lewis Hall, then (a) I disagree, and (b) Everton should definitely have had one when Schär upended Barry.

I got the feeling that the crowd turned last night, or at least started to. At full time – despite Newcastle’s late rally – the mood was reminiscent of the dark days of McClaren and Bruce. Fans are running out of patience with the manager and the team. Personally, I’d stick with Jaissle and give him time, but I understand those who are ready to see him go.

I don’t believe we’ll be in a relegation scrap but nor do I believe we’ll be troubling any teams outside of England next season. We would have gone seventh (net 6th if Manchester City receive the expected points deduction) if we’d won last night. Instead, a team with limited ambitions vaulted above us into that position. And deserved to.

Lukáš Horníček 4 Actually made a couple of good saves second half, but only after he allowed the ball to squirm under his body to the feet of a grateful Thierno Barry, who could not miss.

Amar Dedić 4 Had a couple of runs upfield but didn’t know what to do when he got there. Other than that, I don’t remember him doing much at all. I don’t know enough about football to say that he was complicit in the poor defending that led to Everton’s goal but it wasn’t a good look.

Fabian Schär 4 Went down too easily when Barry scored, hoping to win a free kick. Didn’t get it. Could easily have conceded a pen when he took the legs of the same player. He looked out of sorts. His passing – usually a strength – was poor.

Dan Burn 6 Showed tenacity, desire and leadership when others showed none of those things. Wasn’t immune to a bit of panicking but not as much as some of his colleagues.

Lewis Hall 6 OK overall. At least he tried. By the end of the game, he was playing almost as a midfielder trying to get things going.

Nico Gonzàlez 3 His poorest game for us. No presence, no authority, and displaying a lack of belief that spread through the team. If he’d come from Stoke City on a free, you’d say he wasn’t good enough on this form.

Joelinton 5 I see him getting pelters in some quarters today but I thought he was a lot better than Nico. Tried to initiate some attacks and looked more interested than most. He didn’t have a great game but at least he didn’t hide.

Anthony Elanga 3 Elanga is back to the version we saw last season. Creates very little, loses the ball too easily, looks ordinary. And completely failed to track Tyrique George as he sauntered into our area to set up Everton’s goal. He was meant to be an upgrade on Murphy, and apart from a couple of times, he’s never really looked like it.

Joe Willock 4 Started quite brightly compared to many, but began to fade, and then kept fading.

Harvey Barnes 5 Kept going. Showed a willingness to get on the ball and attack our opponents more than most. Not a great game. If he had been taking an exam, he’d get a pass mark, but no more.

William Osula 5 He doesn’t lack enthusiasm and that is a good thing. What he lacked last night was service and awareness. Made the wrong runs a few times and made the wrong decision on others. That he hardly saw the ball was not all his fault.

Sean Steur 7 Our Player of the Match and he was only on for half an hour.

Instantly improved our attacking options, playing passes through the Everton defence, and showing a composure that those with a decade more experience did not. I guess the manager wants to protect him, given our current plight and Steur’s tender years, but he is a baller, and he needs to start. If not now, when?

Yoane Wissa 4 Well, he had – I think – our first and second shots on target, but he fluffed his lines. I have some sympathy for Wissa – against a side like Everton, who packed the area at 1-0, and whose defenders are massive, a small, quick striker like him is always going to be at a disadvantage. But he needs to improve his shooting.

Jacob Ramsey 2 I thought he looked pretty good when he joined the fray. Positive, combative and determined. I thought he’d scored at one point – my arms were in the air – but it whistled past the post. 10 minutes later he was in the shower after two yellows in almost record time. The second one – which could have been a red – was inexcusable. It just capped off an awful night.

Jacob Murphy 5 Didn’t stand out, but was better than many of his team mates, including the player he replaced. Kept the Everton defence interested.

Bazoumana Touré 6 I know he ‘wasn’t on long enough to judge’ but he looked better than just about everyone bar Steur.

Livened up the team, livened up the crowd. If I was Jaissle, I’d throw caution to the wind and start him and Steur. Our regular starters look jaded.

#2107. Andoni Iraola wishes Alexander Isak had done one thing differently in Liverpool defeat

Andoni Iraola is convinced that Liverpool would ‘100%’ have been awarded a penalty on Sunday if Alexander Isak had gone to ground after having his shirt pulled by Jurrien Timber.

The Reds’ head coach was left bewildered over that incident in the 21st minute of the Reds’ 1-0 defeat at home to Arsenal, for whom Kai Havertz had scored just five minutes earlier.

Neither Andy Madley nor the officials on VAR duty felt that a spot kick was warranted, a decision which was met with unified disagreement from Jamie Carragher, Ian Wright and Daniel Sturridge on Sky Sports.

Speaking to Sky Sports after the match, Iraola felt that the incident was a ‘clear penalty’ and believes that a foul would’ve been given had Isak gone down when Timber pulled his shirt.

The Liverpool boss said: “The fact that you are even asking me that he should have gone to the floor, that’s the thing. If he goes to the floor, they call the penalty for me. They call the penalty 100%.”

When the interviewer asked the Basque whether he’d tell Isak to go to ground if that happens again, he replied: “Yes, definitely.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

We now have a farcical situation whereby Iraola feels compelled to openly advocate for his players to go to ground under contact from opponents because the officials on duty are failing in their task.

Quite frankly, Isak shouldn’t feel any obligation to engineer a penalty in such situations, seeing as the shirt tug from Timber was so blatantly obvious that there’s no justification for those on VAR not to intervene, whatever about the on-field referee missing it.

It’s the striker’s job to try and get on the end of the ball coming into the box (which he probably would’ve done if his jersey wasn’t pulled), not to seek the manufacturing of a spot kick because the officials can’t be trusted to do their job of calling such clear fouls.

That decision felt significant in the overall context of the match yesterday. Had the referee awarded the penalty as he should’ve done, Liverpool would’ve had a chance to quickly cancel out Havertz’s goal.

Had they done so, we can’t help but feel that it would’ve been a rather different game at Anfield. Obviously that’ll forever remain hypothetical, but there’s a real sense of what might’ve been had the officials not erred so badly over the incident involving Isak and Timber.

#2106. Scotland star eyes dream Nou Camp return after childhood visit

Aston Villa captain John McGinn does not want the Champions League clash with Barcelona to be another tourist trip to the Nou Camp.

The Scotland international went on a stadium tour as an eight-year-old when he was on holiday in nearby Salou and remembers it as the day Ricardo Quaresma signed for the LaLiga club in 2003.

But on Tuesday he will be leading Villa out at the famous stadium as the club’s remarkable journey under Unai Emery continues, which has seen them beat Bayern Munich and Paris St Germain in the Champions League and win the Europa League.

McGinn admits he is living out his childhood dream, but wants matches like this to be a regular occurence.

“I used to go on holiday to Salou, and I was here for the stadium tour the day that Ricardo Quaresma signed for Barcelona, so I think I was eight years old,” McGinn said.

“I’ve never been since, but tomorrow night I’ll be excited to represent Aston Villa on the big stage.

“I am 32 years old. The trajectory of this club is allowing me to dream the same way I dreamed since I was 9, 10 and 11, to play in front of the biggest crowds in the biggest arenas and obviously this is a very historic stadium.

“But what the club are trying to do now is make this normal, make this a yearly experience and make Aston Villa compete with the best in England and the best in Europe.

“So it’s a pleasure to be on this journey with the supporters. I’m sure they’ll enjoy tonight and tomorrow.

“But as professionals, we only enjoy the experience if we have three points and that’s what we’ll be trying to do.”

Villa have won their opening three matches of the league phase, but face their stiffest test yet.

Being back at the Nou Camp probably will not bring back as many happy memories for Emery as it will McGinn as the scars of the 2017 ‘Remontada’ still loom large.

Emery was in charge of PSG when they squandered a 4-0 first-leg lead in the last 16 after a harrowing 6-1 defeat in Barcelona, where the hosts scored two goals in injury time.

The Spaniard looked like a man who is yet to exoricse his demons when asked about it ahead of the match.

Asked what he learned from that experience, he said: “(It was) one match more. Everything that happened in that match I learned in my career.

“I started coaching in 2004, 22 years in a row. Played in Europe 16 years in a row, different competitions, Champions League, Europa League and Conference League, and I’ve learned in all of the competitions.

“And in that match I learned so, so much. One sport side and another not a sport side. The necessity of VAR for football in that moment. The necessity of VAR.”

Emery has lost 14 of 15 visits to the Nou Camp as a manager and says Barca are the favourites for the match.

“To play against Barcelona is to play against the elite,” he said. “Barcelona is among the favourite to win the Champions League, I could pick five teams vying for the title, and they are one of them.

“Barcelona have six points, we have nine, they lost to PSG. To play against PSG is demanding, it was a clash between two favourites.

“We need to adapt, but we need to play our own game.”

#2105. Duo escape criticism after West Ham slow start shocker against Baggies | West Ham News

Two names seemed – deservedly – absent from the long list of players singled out for culpability amongst the anger and consternation felt across fan channels and the wider football media this weekend, as pre-season favourites West Ham slumped to their third home defeat of the season.

Jarrod Bowen, without saying, put in a shift and dragged the Hammers back once with a trademark run and low shot: But two of West Ham’s youngsters both put in solid shifts, despite the result, and are deserving of warmer words than the rest of the starting line up.

Edvin Austbø, starting in place of Manor Solomon, injected pace and directness on the left hand side that was deserving of praise -yet his efforts were largely lost amongst the justifiable criticism of the team’s performance.

West Ham’s Edvin Austbø – another one who escaped criticism amidst a crap team performance

Playing alongside the tentative Maximilian Kilman would tax the abilities of any decent centre half and it is vital for West Ham’s future that he doesn’t find himself banished back to the u21’s after one start and a result that reflects badly on the whole team.

There was considerable fan encouragement for the youngster and I’d certainly pick him ahead of Max Kilman on present form.

These young players are the future of the club and need an arm around their shoulders after both put in a shift: The pair should certainly hold their heads up high and expect further first team outings, after neither of the duo let their manager, their team mates or the supporters down.

#2104. The Strange Pattern Behind Every Major West Ham Managerial Appointment

A social media post doing the rounds over the weekend has sparked an interesting debate among West Ham supporters, highlighting what some see as a recurring theme in the club’s managerial appointments under David Sullivan and the late David Gold.

The post lists a succession of West Ham managers and jokingly categorises them by their playing positions:

The less charitable description attached to Avram Grant is perhaps best left where it belongs, on social media. He actually never played professional football!

While the observation is obviously tongue-in-cheek, it does raise an intriguing point. Since Sullivan and Gold took control of West Ham in 2010, the club has overwhelmingly turned to former defenders and goalkeepers when appointing managers.

Defenders and goalkeepers are often associated with organisation, structure and caution. Many of the managers West Ham have appointed during the ownership era have certainly prioritised defensive solidity first and attacking football second.

Bilic – one in a long line of defenders or ‘keepers appointed as West Ham Manager

That said, West Ham have hardly looked defensively secure under Nuno this season, and many teams have taken full advantage of those weaknesses.

Allardyce built his reputation on pragmatism. Moyes delivered the most successful period of the modern era through discipline, shape and resilience. Even Pellegrini, despite his reputation for attacking football at Manchester City, spent much of his West Ham spell battling to find defensive balance.

The goalkeeper connection is perhaps even more interesting. Both Lopetegui and Nuno Espírito Santo were former keepers, with each enjoying success elsewhere before taking on the challenge in east London.

Of course, there is no evidence that Sullivan sat down with a shortlist and immediately crossed off every former midfielder or striker. Football management success rarely comes down to the position someone played during their career.

After all, some of the Premier League’s most successful modern managers have come from every area of the pitch.

Yet supporters often look for patterns when results are poor, and West Ham’s recent struggles have inevitably led to fresh examination of decision-making at boardroom level.

Whether the theory is meaningful or merely an amusing statistical quirk, one thing is certain, Hammers fans would probably care far less about a manager’s former position if the current team was climbing the Championship table.

Sometimes football’s strangest observations turn out to be nothing more than coincidence. This may well be one of them. But it is the sort of coincidence that will get supporters talking.

I have been a season ticket holder since the late eighties, so experienced the highs and lows of being a West Ham supporter. I previously wrote for OLAS and have contributed to a number of football publications in the past.

What do you expect when you have unambitious, dullard, embarrassing, two bob, cheapo, gobby owners; you get tinpot appointments.

Loser managers that are unemployed and no-one else wants.

Even the reappointment of Moyes was an embarrassing and two bob appointment at the time as he’d been jobless since his first stint with us.

It was pure chance and an absolute fluke that he did well for us.

Pellegrini was the only ambitious appointment, and even that was only forced due to rioting from our supporters due to the owners lies and lack of ambition.

The sooner David Sullivan and his sons have no involvement in the club, the better.

He doesn’t look in the best of health, and he won’t be here forever.

I can think of something else which all those former and present West Ham managers might have in common. They were all unemployed and probably had all been sacked!

Strange how many of them were unable to see our defensive frailties over the years, although when Stuart Pearce was employed as first team coach we did look much more solid at the back.

the other thing that they have in common, with the exception of Moyes is they’re all absolute rubbish. ( being nice).

#2103. If West Ham Cannot Sack Nuno – Then He Must Make These Immediate Changes

Calls for West Ham United manager Nuno Espírito Santo to be sacked are growing louder following consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion. The Hammers have dropped to eighth in the Championship, and supporters are understandably questioning whether the Portuguese coach is capable of leading the club back to the Premier League.

I certainly fall squarely into the camp of people who don’t believe Nuno can either motivate his players or outsmart many of his rival Championship managers. The football has become stale, the team looks disjointed and there is precious little evidence of a manager getting the best out of what should be a very competitive squad.

But if we’re absolutely honest with ourselves, I suspect most West Ham supporters would acknowledge that Nuno is nowhere near being sacked. So rather than simply demanding his removal, perhaps the more useful question is what he can actually change to get this team playing better.

There are several reasons why I suspect Espírito Santo will remain in charge for the foreseeable future.

Firstly, West Ham are still in a state of flux regarding the club’s ownership structure. Until the proposed changes involving Vanessa Gold’s shareholding are completed and the i’s are dotted and t’s crossed, there remains uncertainty about precisely who will be making the biggest decisions.

Secondly, despite bringing in the best part of £200million through summer player sales, there are questions about how much money the club actually has available. Whether West Ham would be willing or able to fund another managerial dismissal and appointment is unclear.

And thirdly, if Daniel Křetínský is indeed calling the shots, Nuno is very much the manager he backed to lead the club through this Championship campaign.

Which leaves us with a rather uncomfortable situation. A manager whose football is becoming increasingly difficult to defend, but who may nevertheless be extremely secure in his job.

The first thing I’d change is the defence.

Nuno needs to abandon the experiment of playing Morato at left-back and select a proper full-back in that position.

I appreciate that Morato has performed reasonably well at times, and his versatility has been useful. But ultimately he’s a central defender, and I don’t believe the arrangement is helping West Ham develop a balanced team.

Whether Nuno selects Adama Boiro or Ollie Scarles doesn’t particularly matter to me at this stage.

We need better balance, more natural movement down the left and defenders playing in positions they understand.

As I’ve said previously, Arne Engels appears to be guaranteed a game irrespective of how he performs. Meanwhile, Nuno seems to believe he can win the Championship without consistently selecting a recognised defensive midfielder.

West Ham have a wealth of options in central midfield, yet we repeatedly find ourselves overrun, unable to retain possession and exposed whenever opponents break forward.

For that reason, I think it’s probably time to change the midfield completely.

I’d be tempted to give Lewis Orford another opportunity alongside either Edson Álvarez or Soungoutou Magassa.

Both Álvarez and Magassa offer the possibility of greater defensive protection, something West Ham have been desperately lacking.

And with a more secure base behind him, Divine Mukasa could finally be deployed in his best position as a number ten.

He’s a wonderfully gifted young footballer, but we’re wasting too much of his ability by asking him to drop deep and collect possession from the centre-backs.

Get him further up the pitch, give him some protection behind him and let him start opening up opposition defences.

Between the sticks, Mads Hermansen hasn’t exactly covered himself in glory.

I’m not suggesting every goal West Ham concede is his fault, because the defending in front of him has frequently been dreadful.

But when a team is struggling this badly, nobody should be guaranteed their place simply because they’ve been selected regularly.

Nuno has an ex PCG goalkeeper in Alphonse Areola at his disposal… surely it’s worth a try?

Which brings us to the striking department.

Leading up to the Southampton game, plenty of people were keen to repeat the fallacy that West Ham couldn’t win football matches without Pablo.

It’s worth remembering that Pablo didn’t start the Hammers’ 6-0 victory against Wrexham, which I consider our most convincing performance of the season.

And following back-to-back defeats in which the £23million striker started both matches, I suspect that particular myth has been exposed to all but his most vociferous supporters.

I don’t question Pablo’s effort. He works hard, puts himself about and certainly isn’t afraid of making a tackle.

Unfortunately, those qualities alone don’t make somebody an effective Championship striker.

For that reason, I’d be inclined to give Joël Piroe, our only proven Championship goalscorer among the recognised centre-forwards, a proper opportunity to establish himself.

He hasn’t been given anything resembling a consistent run in the side, and I struggle to understand how Nuno can properly assess his options without giving him one.

I’m not suggesting Piroe is guaranteed to solve our problems.

Of course, all these changes will count for very little unless Nuno can find a way to motivate his players.

I have little doubt that West Ham possess a number of talented footballers, many of whom I suspect would look considerably better under different coaches.

Once the players cross that white line, tactics, organisation and selection become equally important.

And that is where Nuno continues to let himself down.

Whether any of my suggestions would make a significant difference, I genuinely don’t know.

But I do know that repeating the same errors time and again isn’t going to get West Ham back into contention for automatic promotion.

The players who have consistently underperformed need to be dropped, and those who haven’t had much of an opportunity deserve a chance.

We have enough players in this squad to try something different.

And frankly, that’s probably the best we can hope for at the moment.

Because as much as some West Ham supporters might wish for Nuno Espírito Santo’s removal, I suspect he’s currently extremely secure in his job.

Which means if West Ham are going to improve, the manager who created many of these problems is probably going to have to be the one who solves them.

#2102. “I’m asking myself why…” – Steve Nicol frustrated by one thing Iraola did in Liverpool defeat

Steve Nicol was left frustrated by one tactical decision from Andoni Iraola during Liverpool’s defeat to Arsenal on Sunday.

The match was settled by Kai Havertz’s goal in the 16th minute and contained some controversial flashpoints, including a blatant penalty that the Reds should’ve been awarded and some unwelcome theatrics from Alexis Mac Allister after a clash with Noni Madueke.

Despite being on the losing side, the hosts were competitive for most of the game at Anfield, and it wasn’t until the surprise withdrawal of Trey Nyoni just before the hour mark that they began to lose the impetus they had in the middle of the park.

Speaking on ESPN FC as he reflected on the match, Nicol felt that Iraola’s substitution of the teenager for Dominik Szoboszlai was a poor decision.

The ex-Liverpool defender said: “The one thing that frustrates me more than anything else is the substitution that Iraola made after 60 minutes.

“Other than the little spell in the first half just before and just after Arsenal’s goal, Liverpool were dominating the game. Mac Allister and Nyoni had locked the midfield up and Arsenal were under pressure.

“It was the same at the start of the second half, and when he made the substitution and brought Nyoni off and Szoboszlai on, I’m asking myself why is he not taking Wirtz off and leaving Mac Allister and Nyoni to dominate the way they have been. From that point on, this game changed.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

We agree with Nicol that the decision to withdraw Nyoni – who’d been enjoying a terrific game on his first Premier League start – seemed surprising at the time and, in hindsight, wasn’t a smart move by Iraola.

We’d understand it a bit more if the 19-year-old was on a yellow card and in danger of being sent off, although we’ll admit that he was fortunate to avoid going in the book for a couple of aggressive fouls early in the match.

While possession stats can sometimes be misleading, it seems indicative that Liverpool had 59.9% of the ball at the time that the teenager was substituted, and 56.4% by full-time (WhoScored), a notable drop-off after Nyoni’s withdrawal as the Reds lost a measure of control in the middle of the park.

Florian Wirtz – the player that Nicol had wanted to be subbed off instead – has been excellent in recent weeks but didn’t exert as much influence yesterday, and the midfield was much less balanced with him and Szoboszlai on the pitch for the final half-hour.

Whatever you make of Iraola’s substitutions, it’s a testament to how brilliantly Nyoni is doing that Liverpool lost impetus after he went off, and the case for keeping him in the starting XI has been strengthened after Sunday.

#2100. The ‘biggest trick’ Celtic missed that could come back to haunt them

Martin O’Neill’s position at Celtic has come under fresh scrutiny following a run of six defeats in 10 matches.

The club remains top of the Premiership, but former Rangers midfielder Kevin Thomson believes the club missed a huge opportunity in the summer by keeping O’Neill as manager rather than moving him into a different role.

Speaking on The Breakdown alongside former Celtic defender Charlie Mulgrew, Thomson claimed Celtic should have appointed then-Motherwell boss Jens Berthel Askou and kept O’Neill around as a mentor or sounding board for the new manager.

Thomson said: “I do think, and it’s easy with hindsight, I did think how dramatic the last day of the season was, he should’ve just up sticks and left. But I still felt the club would be missing a trick.

“I think Martin would’ve been a brilliant foil, mentor or sounding board, somebody to speak to, somebody to confide in as part of whatever that looked like for Celtic, for the new manager coming in.

“Now he’s been the manager; he’s had it for a longer period of time rather than just short-term, you kind of feel as though Martin O’Neill wouldn’t work because he’s now attached himself to being the manager.”

O’Neill had led Celtic to the title last season after returning as manager, with the Hoops beating Hearts on the final day to seal the championship. He was already in the job on a permanent basis, while Askou left Motherwell to take charge of Toulouse.

Rangers-daft pundit sounds Celtic alarm with ‘Covid year’ warning

Celtic's tactics under Martin O'Neill torn apart as ‘biggest pet hate’ laid bare

Ex-Celtic star sends fresh Scotland message after stunning display

Mulgrew believes Celtic could instead have installed Askou as manager and found a different position for O’Neill.

He said: “If he walks away then, Celtic still weighed him in with good money because he deserved that because of what he did with the title and then gave it to a Berthel Askou and let Martin O’Neill be director of football or be on the board or whatever.”

Thomson was even more emphatic about Celtic’s failure to move for Askou. He said: “It’s the biggest trick Celtic have ever missed, not getting him.”

Mulgrew added: “It’s a big one, isn’t it? I think he would have been desperate for it.

Thomson believes Askou could have been well suited to Celtic given the resources available at Parkhead and the style of football supporters have been accustomed to. He added: “You think of the resources that he would’ve had at his disposal and the type of players.

“He would be as close as getting a replacement that I think Celtic fans have been pining for since Ange Postecoglou.”

#2099. Nuno Espírito Santo is sacked as former Newcastle star set to take over at West Ham

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Nuno Espírito Santo has been sacked by West Ham.

An official club statement on Tuesday morning revealing the news.

Nuno Espírito Santo sacked with West Ham sitting eighth in the Championship, six points behind league leaders Middlesbrough and the Hammers only two points off third.

The official club statement beginning: ‘West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team Head Coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect. Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the Board of Directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the Club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.’

Nuno Espírito Santo managed just over 13 months with the Hammers, having arrived late September 2025.

The official West Ham statement going on to say: ‘Assistant Head Coach Rui Pedro Silva and Goalkeeper Coach Rui Barbosa have also departed. West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the Club, and wish them all the very best for the future. The process of recruiting a new Head Coach is already underway. Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of squad preparations ahead of tomorrow evening’s EFL Championship fixture at Cardiff City, and the Club will make no further comment until the appointment of the new Head Coach is confirmed.’

David Ornstein at The Athletic has reported that former Newcastle United star Scott Parker has already agreed to take over at West Ham.

Parker also played for the Hammers back in the day.

#2098. The night Newcastle United stole the sun from my heart

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Watching the latest Newcastle United match against Everton on TV, I turned to the missus after 10 minutes and said: “We’re not gonna win this one.”

My verdict was less than insightful; anyone inside St James’ Park on Monday night would have quickly realised the visitors looked the better team and were seemingly playing with an extra man, such was their early control.

Matthais Jassle fronted up in post-match interviews but there was little comfort in his words. “It’s not easy to explain as it looked so good during the week [in training]. The lads looked committed and the confidence was there. Today from the start the confidence was missing. We need to improve really fast. We have to encourage them that they are able to do it, that they have the potential to play in that way.”

The task of restoring confidence is a tough gig for any manager, never mind one whose experience of coaching in the Premier League was as comprehensive as mine only three months ago.

Apart from the encounters with an undercooked Liverpool and a hapless Tottenham, there have been only glimpses of “the Jaissle way” this season. We started like thoroughbreds against the previously unbeaten Hull City, then ran out of energy. We blew away Crystal Palace in the 15 minutes immediately after the interval at a windswept Selhurst Park, having produced a first half of dire quality.

The head coach says he sees the players do it in training. That’s worth diddly squat once they cross the white line and are confronted not by their mates but by opponents determined to make us second best. Everton have done it twice, so have Villa, Coventry and Leeds United.

Time for a history lesson. In the mid-70s, the Mackems bought a young winger called Tom Finney. No, not the Preston plumber. This one was a Northern Irishman who played a total of 15 games at Joker Park before leaving for Cambridge United, whom he served with distinction, scoring 56 times in 268 appearances.

So what’s all that got to do with the price of fish? Well, Finney was the subject of an article in the Chronicle by Len Hetherington (the Sunderland version of the great John Gibson) in which the footballer was described as having every quality needed to be a big success. There was just one problem: those abundant skills were seen every time he trained but come match day he was deeply underwhelming.

Which reminds me of an oft-cited quote by the baseball legend Yogi Berra: “Ninety per cent of the game is half-mental.” Even those who struggle with maths should be able to get the drift. An awful lot of competitive sport is played in the head. There’s little difference between confidence and belief. They are almost synonyms. Our German coach says the players are lacking confidence. I suspect belief is the missing ingredient: the players are struggling to believe he is the answer to the question set when Eddie Howe walked away.

Jaissle is 38, with a cv showing success in the Austrian league and in Saudi Arabia. The latter is regarded by most football fans as a vanity project by the Saudi Arabia PIF (who just happen to be the majority owners of Newcastle United). I have not watched even one minute of action, despite the dubious attraction of the preening Portuguese poster boy. My bad!

As for the Austrian League, 11 years ago I found myself in that country’s fascinating capital city. A bit of essential research told me the Prater Park (where the big wheel featured in The Third Man, a 1949 film noir, still slowly turns) was home to Rapid Vienna. They had been runners-up to Red Bull Salzburg in the 2014-15 league. They were top of the table. They were hosting one of their biggest rivals, so what’s a football follower to do?

Leaving Lady R to explore the many other attractions of the area, I headed for the stadium.

The match was dreadful, almost as bad as the first half at Palace last month. The fans spent much of the afternoon goading each other rather than watching the ball, a response quite understandable because of the quality , or lack of, on show. No attempts on target from either side until I broke the habit of a lifetime and walked out with five minutes left. Inevitably, the hosts, whom I had already renamed Vapid Vienna, scored a late, late winner.

For the record, Red Bull Salzburg won the Austrian Bundesliga title for 10 consecutive seasons from 2014, including two when the head coach was Herr Jaissle. That gives some perspective to his achievements.

The other highlight of that day (apart from a failed rendezvous blamed on the presence of a second big wheel in the Prater Park and confusion over Central European Time) was a conversation with the hotel receptionist.

When I asked if she was a fan and said I had just been to watch the league leaders, she looked bemused. “Yes, I am, but not of Austrian football. Why did you go? It’s rubbish.”

OK, that was only one match and the opinion of only one local . . . but maybe she was spot-on. The lesser-known Bundesliga is a long way down the pecking order of Uefa competitions.

Hiring a manager who won two titles there is clearly better than hiring a manager without any honours. Are his medals enough to convince battle-hardened Premier League players, though? The evidence so far suggests that question has not been answered in the affirmative.

We all know there are explanations for the bumps in the road. Our best players sold, even if at least two of them were not at their best last season. Raw young recruits brought in as replacements, though Hornicek, Dedic and Gonzalez were the only summer signings in last night’s line-up. All three are experienced compared with Steur and Toure, who outshone all their teammates despite playing cameo roles.

What is the biggest, most relevant explanation? A lot of supporters are looking no further than the head coach.

Jamie Smith’s excellent match report paints a picture of woe that is difficult to dispute. I’ll be at Craven Cottage on Saturday for a non-televised, 3pm traditional kick-off, thanks to a person who knows a person who has a spare ticket.

Perhaps my first appearance in the away end at Fulham for 47 seasons will bring United a change of fortune.

Until then, there’s a catchily annoying song flying around my brain like a moth trapped in old Mother Hubbard’s cupboard. The seemingly endless summer has finally given way to autumn storms in West Sussex. There’s a chill in the morning air. Twenty months on from the greatest day in the club’s modern history, all I can hear is James Dean Bradfield singing: “You stole the sun from my heart.”

At least he adds: “I love you all the same.”

#2095. ‘You need to improve…’ – Ex-PGMOL chief urges Howard Webb to act after Anfield controversy

Pro Ref chief executive Howard Webb has been urged to take drastic action after some controversial flashpoints at Anfield on Sunday.

Liverpool’s 1-0 defeat to Arsenal was pockmarked by incidents such as the Reds being denied a blatant penalty when Jurrien Timber clearly tugged Alexander Isak’s shirt inside the box, and Alexis Mac Allister going to ground theatrically after mild contact from Noni Madueke’s forehead.

The home fans in L4 vented their spleen at referee Andy Madley as he left the pitch after full-time, and one former top-flight official believes that the 43-year-old should be demonstrably penalised for his performance on Merseyside yesterday.

Keith Hackett was surprised that the Yorkshire native was appointed to such a high-profile figure and said that, if it were up to him, the whistler would be stood down from Premier League duty next weekend.

The former PGMOL chief told Football Insider: “I was surprised, having watched his recent performances, that Andy Madley was appointed to this game. We have elite referees within the group. We have a pecking order, and those referees that are in form should get this game.

“There are going to be knocks on the door saying, ‘Boss, why haven’t I got a game?’; and I would be saying, ‘You need to improve your performance and be more consistent’.

“I don’t think he had his best game, and I don’t know what his best game is. We’ve highlighted a number of ifs, and I’ve highlighted one that is 100% incorrect. That says to me, next week if I was doing the appointments, he [isn’t getting] a game.”

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Some media outlets highlighted in the days leading up to Sunday’s fixture that it was Madley’s first appointment to a Premier League fixture between clubs in the traditional ‘big six’ for more than two years, with eyebrows being raised at that decision from Webb.

Some of the referees who are regarded as among the best in England have had their share of controversial moments too, so we had no complaints with the 43-year-old getting the Liverpool-Arsenal game, but he did himself no favours yesterday.

How he (and especially Stuart Attwell on VAR) can stand over the failure to award a penalty for Timber’s clear shirt tug on Isak is a mystery – that was a major error which wasn’t corrected when the opportunity arose, and it had significant consequences for the game as a whole.

Had the spot kick been awarded in the 21st minute (shortly after Kai Havertz scored) and the Reds equalised, the momentum of the match could’ve swung substantially. Andoni Iraola will surely have felt that way afterwards.

In his role as the head of Pro Ref, Webb bears ultimately responsiblity for ensuring high standards of officiating in the Premier League, something which hasn’t been the case for as long as we can remember.

If Madley is removed from top-flight duty next weekend, he could have no complaints after his error-strewn performance at Anfield on Sunday.

With the exception of a couple of referees, the current batch are not up to standard. It is time to bring in referees from outside the UK to officiate in high profile matches. Having to apologise every time a referee gets it wrong – which is happening quite regularly with Liverpool and costing them yet more points – isn’t enough. It’s very clear that the refereeing needs to be a lot better.

#2094. Kretinsky faces challenge to show he’s no David Sullivan 2.0 | West Ham News

West Ham’s last three managers have all faced a gradual, game-by-game countdown of deadlines, drama and demands for improvement, which all failed and eventually led to their demise. Who can forget the painful series of ‘must win’ games that both Lopetegui and Graham Potter endured – seemingly without an end – as David Sullivan kicked the can down the road rather than making clear cut, cold, calculating decision to cut the ties with a failing manager.

Sullivan in fact became something of a laughing stock after proclaiming ‘this one is a must – win‘ and then famously  sitting on his hands and not sacking Potter after he’d duly failed to win.

Of course the irony was that all three were dispatched eventually – in differing circumstances but dispatched nonetheless.

How many points would have been saved if Sullivan had fired Potter earlier on in the season?

Worst ever, yet stumbled on with endless ‘must win games’ to try and improve results: Graham Potter was fired eventually anyway and quite possibly the delay cost West Ham their Premier League status

Not just my opinion, but pretty much the favour of the lunchtime West Ham YouTube channels too – that Kretinsky needs to be bold and decisive and prove he’s not simply following the David Sullivan modus operandi and merely kicking the Management can down the road.

A bad manager doesn’t suddenly become one worth saving  merely because of a possible lucky win away at Cardiff on Wednesday night, as Russ from the west ham network points out today in his video entitled “Why are West Ham waiting to sack Nuno| That’s not leadership, that’s indecision”

In essence, Kretinsky – who shies away from the limelight, but according to our own Gonzo on hammers chat, has something of a record of being ruthless with his firing of managers over at Sparta Prague. The Sphinx needs to bring that ruthlessness to bear at West Ham and prove he’s not merely a carbon copy of the former chairman – a David Sullivan 2.0.

Kicking the managerial can down the road merely to save a few million in compensation is a false economy, with promotion to the Premier League reportedly being worth £200 million. Automatic promotion, the club’s stated aim, is looking a very unlikely possibility under Nuno, with West Ham on a downward dive and currently in eighth position.

Nuno Espírito Santo has had over a year in charge yet still can’t get his side playing positive, attacking, fear-free football, even in the second division.

#2093. Ex-Celtic star’s £22m move takes fresh twist as manager who signed him axed

Arne Engels faces a fresh period of uncertainty at West Ham after the club sacked Nuno Espirito Santo just months after his £22 million move from Celtic.

The former Hoops midfielder has started every Championship game since making the switch to the London Stadium, with Nuno having been a major backer of the Belgian.

Club statement. Read more: https://t.co/LT0TZXbSpR https://t.co/0r6Yz55iRi

— West Ham United (@WestHam) November 3, 2026

But West Ham have now decided to make a change following back-to-back home defeats, leaving the club eighth in the Championship.

Saturday’s 3-1 loss to West Brom prompted what the Hammers described as a “thorough review” of their start to life in the second tier.

The club had opted to stick with Nuno in May despite his failure to preserve their Premier League status, but the Portuguese coach has now been removed from his position.

The managerial change provides an intriguing twist for Arne Engels, who only left Celtic for West Ham in August.

The Belgian made the move in a £22m deal after Celtic rejected two earlier bids, with Martin O’Neill admitting at the time that Engels wanted the transfer and did not want to risk injury by playing in the Hoops’ Champions League play-off.

Martin O’Neill also described the midfielder’s departure as “disappointing” and conceded his running power would be difficult for Celtic to replace.

The ‘biggest trick’ Celtic missed that could come back to haunt them

Rangers-daft pundit sounds Celtic alarm with ‘Covid year’ warning

Celtic's tactics under Martin O'Neill torn apart as ‘biggest pet hate’ laid bare

Arne Engels has since been a regular under Nuno, starting every league match following his arrival, but will now have to impress whoever takes charge next.

West Ham said: “West Ham United can confirm that men’s first-team head coach Nuno Espírito Santo has left his position with immediate effect.

“Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club’s objectives and expectations remain on track.

“Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also departed.

“West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.

“The process of recruiting a new head coach is already underway.”

Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of preparations for Wednesday night’s Championship trip to Cardiff City.

#2092. Nuno’s West Ham Future Under Threat As Board Concerns Grow

Nuno Espírito Santo’s position as West Ham United manager is under increasing threat, according to a new report from The Guardian. With the Hammers slipping to eighth in the Championship following consecutive home defeats, patience is reportedly wearing thin among key figures at the London Stadium.

Writing for The Guardian, Hammers fan Jacob Steinberg reports that although Nuno is expected to be given more time to turn things around, influential figures at West Ham are becoming increasingly impatient with the club’s disappointing start to the season.

The report comes just two days after the 3-1 defeat against West Bromwich Albion, a result which prompted further questions about Nuno’s tactics and his ability to get the best out of a squad assembled with the intention of securing an immediate return to the Premier League.

According to The Guardian, any decision regarding Nuno’s future would be taken collectively by the West Ham board, rather than by one shareholder acting alone.

Interim chief executive Karim Virani and recruitment director Nils Koppen are among those expected to have input.

The report also revisits the decision to retain Nuno following relegation, explaining that David Sullivan had wanted a change of manager while Daniel Křetínský favoured continuity.

However, that previous support does not necessarily mean the manager’s position is secure indefinitely.

West Ham have won just twice in their last six Championship matches, and the upcoming fixtures against Cardiff City and Blackburn Rovers could become increasingly important ahead of the November international break.

The Guardian also highlights concerns about Nuno’s inability to settle on his strongest starting eleven, the lack of balance in midfield and the failure of the club’s strikers to provide sufficient goals.

The report states that West Ham’s three recognised centre-forwards, Joël Piroe, Pablo Felipe and Taty Castellanos, have scored just five league goals between them this season.

Meanwhile, Jarrod Bowen has scored seven, leaving the Hammers heavily dependent on our captain.

The continued absence of recognised defensive midfielders Soungoutou Magassa and Edson Álvarez from Nuno’s preferred selections is another issue raised.

These concerns will sound familiar to Claret & Hugh readers. Following the West Brom defeat, I questioned whether Nuno’s entire West Ham project was becoming fundamentally flawed, particularly given the lack of cohesion and the manager’s constant tactical changes.

And while I appreciate that managers need time, I struggle to see how West Ham can continue performing so poorly with a squad that should be capable of competing for automatic promotion.

Perhaps the most important aspect of The Guardian’s report is the suggestion that Nuno will face difficult questions if performances fail to improve before the international break.

There is no suggestion that a dismissal has already been agreed, and the report specifically indicates that West Ham still hope the manager can turn things around.

Nevertheless, it appears the pressure is no longer coming exclusively from frustrated supporters.

The next two matches now offer Nuno an opportunity to demonstrate that he can produce a convincing response.

Because as I’ve argued previously, West Ham’s problems haven’t suddenly appeared over the last fortnight. The warning signs have been there for considerably longer.

And if the manager cannot begin addressing them, it is becoming increasingly difficult to see how the club can justify continuing with the same approach.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

#2089. Cardiff v West Ham Preview: Parker Era Beckons After Nuno Sacking

Cardiff City v West Ham United EFL Championship Cardiff City Stadium Wednesday 4 November 2026, 7.45pm GMT

West Ham United’s crucial Championship match at Cardiff City will take place against the backdrop of a dramatic managerial change. Nuno Espírito Santo has been sacked with immediate effect following consecutive home defeats against Southampton and West Bromwich Albion.

Scott Parker is expected to replace him, with discussions at an advanced stage and an official announcement anticipated. However, at the time of writing, West Ham have only confirmed that Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville are preparing the squad for Wednesday night.

The change completely transforms the complexion of a match which had looked capable of determining Nuno’s future. West Ham now travel to Wales looking for an immediate response, a much-needed lift and the first glimpse of what could become Parker’s latest Championship promotion challenge.

Scott Parker knows how to get out of the Championship

West Ham confirmed Nuno’s departure following what the club described as a thorough review of the Championship season. Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left, bringing the Portuguese coach’s reign to a complete end.

The decision is hardly surprising after Saturday’s dreadful 3-1 defeat against West Brom. West Ham showed little motivation, lacked a coherent tactical plan and were repeatedly exposed by a team operating with far greater organisation and purpose.

Nuno leaves the Hammers eighth in the Championship after six victories from 13 league matches. We are six points behind leaders Middlesbrough and four away from the automatic-promotion places, which is not an insurmountable position but is considerably worse than expected.

The official statement explained that the board believed change was necessary to keep the club’s objectives on track. That is difficult to argue with because West Ham’s target was never to scrape into the play-offs; it was to secure an immediate return to the Premier League.

The full announcement confirming Nuno’s departure can be read in West Ham United’s official club statement.

Scott Parker is now expected to become West Ham’s new head coach. The former Hammer has been identified as the leading candidate, with multiple reports suggesting an agreement has been reached and only the formal announcement remains outstanding.

Parker’s record in the Championship is the obvious attraction. He has won promotion with Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley, meaning he understands both the division and the specific challenge West Ham face.

He also knows the club. Parker made 129 appearances for the Hammers between 2007 and 2011, captained the team and won Hammer of the Year in three consecutive seasons.

According to our latest information, Parker’s proposed contract is heavily linked to promotion. He is expected to receive a longer-term opportunity if he takes West Ham up, while the club would retain protection if that objective is not achieved.

The timing creates an unusual situation before Wednesday’s match. West Ham have stated that Noble, Potts and Prenderville are temporarily overseeing preparations, but Parker could still be formally appointed before the squad travels to Wales.

Whether he would immediately take charge from the dugout remains unclear. Even if he does, there will be very little time for Parker to introduce significant tactical changes or properly assess a squad he has not coached.

That means the team will probably have to rely upon a reaction to Nuno’s departure rather than any sophisticated new system. The players can no longer hide behind complaints about the previous manager’s tactics, selections or motivational skills.

This is now an opportunity for them to demonstrate that they are considerably better than recent performances have suggested.

Changing the manager does not automatically correct everything which went wrong against Southampton and West Brom. West Ham remain vulnerable defensively, disjointed in midfield and overly reliant upon Jarrod Bowen in attack.

My preferred formation remains a 4-1-4-1, accompanied by drastic changes. Alphonse Areola deserves an opportunity in goal because Mads Hermansen has not done enough to make himself untouchable.

Joël Veltman should start at right-back, with Airidas Golambeckis partnering Max Kilman if Dinos Mavropanos remains unavailable. Kyle Walker-Peters would play on the left if he recovers from the injury sustained against West Brom, although his fitness remains uncertain.

Soungoutou Magassa should operate as the holding midfielder, providing the defensive protection West Ham have been missing. Lewis Orford and Divine Mukasa would then be free to play ahead of him, rather than being asked to perform roles which do not suit their strengths.

Edvin Austbø and Bowen would provide the width, with Joël Piroe finally receiving a proper opportunity as the central striker. As I argued before Nuno’s dismissal, West Ham need to stop repeating the same selection mistakes.

The managerial upheaval makes an honest predicted XI almost impossible. This is therefore the team I would hand to Parker or the interim coaching staff, subject to Walker-Peters and Mavropanos being declared fit.

Cardiff sit 17th after gaining promotion as League One runners-up last season. Brian Barry-Murphy’s team had been unbeaten in three before suffering a 3-0 defeat at Wolverhampton Wanderers on Saturday.

The Bluebirds could also have up to eight players unavailable. Gabriel Osho is suspended, while Will Fish, Perry Ng, Dylan Lawlor, Calum Chambers, Krystian Bielik, Alex Robertson and Isaak Davies are injury doubts.

That does not guarantee West Ham anything, particularly during a turbulent 24 hours at the club. However, it gives the Hammers a very good opportunity to respond immediately and begin repairing the damage caused by consecutive defeats.

The mood around the squad should already have changed. Players who were overlooked or used incorrectly by Nuno now have the chance to impress a new coaching team, while those who had become automatic selections can no longer take their places for granted.

My original prediction was a 1-1 draw, largely because nothing about West Ham’s recent performances inspired confidence. Nuno’s dismissal introduces the possibility of a reaction, but it does not instantly repair the team’s defensive and attacking problems.

West Ham possess more than enough ability to beat a depleted Cardiff team. The uncertainty is whether the players can produce a coherent performance so soon after a major managerial change.

I expect greater energy and urgency, but I will retain my original prediction until we know whether Parker will be in the dugout and which players are available.

Prediction: Cardiff City 1-1 West Ham United

Supporters travelling to the match can find ticket, parking and transport information in West Ham United’s official Cardiff travel guide.

#2088. Tactical change could revitalise Arne Engels if Nuno is ready to grasp the nettle | West Ham News

Arne Engels needs to be freed from the defensive duties with which he’s weighed down by West Ham’s current formation.

At least, that’s the gist of a report published last night suggesting that the Hammers need an old fashioned defensive midfielder at the heart of their side, to block off teams who at present appear to be able to play through their non-existent defensive shield owing to both Engels and Mukasa venturing too far forward too often.

As the 4thofficial suggested, there’s a remedy already at hand, a player largely ignored by Nuno yet one who could possibly could have a role to play in a more defensively solid West Ham United team, which is, frankly desperate to stop the early goals going in: Recalling defensive midfielder Edson Alvarez.

“From West Ham‘s perspective, reinstating Álvarez should come before abandoning the entire tactical framework. Engels has potential, but expecting the Belgian to provide attacking quality and defensive protection simultaneously places unnecessary pressure on an inexperienced midfield partnership.

Álvarez could give the centre-backs greater protection when attacking full-backs advance, while allowing Engels more freedom to distribute and move forward. That adjustment would address an immediate weakness without forcing another expensive recruitment exercise.”

Many have written off Alvarez as being too slow or too volatile in view of his disciplinary record – which other than an infamous red card against Liverpool – is perhaps not as bad as projected.

Report suggests the scrap- heap midfielder could do a job for Nuno.. if the West Ham manager is  big enough to mend bridges with El Machin

Many Claret and Hugh readers have commented that Nuno’s side needs the extra solidity of a ‘number six’ sitting in front of the back line to which, in truth, Engels doesn’t seem to be best suited.

Perhaps, indeed, rather than abandon the whole ‘tactical framework’ or trying to fit yet another square peg into a round hole, Nuno could grasp the nettle and re-integrate the tailor made defensive minded midfielder Alvarez into his line up.

There’s a down side of course. Dropping one of Mukasa or Kanté  would reduce West Ham’s creativity going forward. It could mean reverting Kanté to the bench blunderbuss role for the second half of games, exactly as he started the season so successfully.

It might make the Irons harder to score against in the first ’45 minutes anyway, Which at the moment couldn’t be such a bad thing. Is Nuno ready to grasp the nettle? Something has to give because right now, ‘hard work’ and ‘talking about it‘ isn’t fixing anything.
