#2058. At the moment of reckoning, England’s old anxiety took hold

All the years that have passed since those red shirts on a summer’s day at a long-gone Wembley Stadium – the humiliations, the occasional triumph, the plentiful servings of self-pity. For a short while in Atlanta it felt like that epoch might finally be ending and all it came down to was managing the last five minutes and whatever the beleaguered referee might add.

A place at a World Cup final was within England’s grasp, a mere 60 years since the last. But just as it loomed into view, already the players and their manager were tracing an old path. The man currently in charge of the England team might be German, the players might be of a generation finessed under bold new coaching ideas, but once more a familiar anxiety took hold. England were minutes from the prize. Yet team and manager were already obeying an old instinct to sabotage the moment.

England had been in retreat long before Lionel Messi served up for Enzo Fernández the goal that would level this World Cup semi-final, and then the second for Lautaro Martínez ,which would propel Argentina forward. Of course, Messi is Messi, and this Argentina team exist to exert his will on games by any means necessary. Yet, as ever, at the moment of reckoning, England demonstrated all the resistance of damp cardboard.

Thomas Tuchel once again reverted to the deep defensive position. Once again, the adapted five-man back line sat on the edge of their area. Against Mexico in the last 16, Tuchel was dismissive of any suggestion he had invited pressure, asking what other option he had with just 10 men. Against Norway in the quarter-finals he did the same, once Erling Haaland was off the pitch. Against Argentina, a team accustomed to playing with it all on the line, such a move was fatal.

Argentina are ahead! 😱A relentless spell of pressure sees Alexis Mac Allister hit the post before ANOTHER Lionel Messi assist sets up Lautaro Martinez to make it 2-1. pic.twitter.com/kVoNouFgKZ

Immediately the supporters in the stands in Atlanta, and in the streets and front rooms of England, recognised the mistake. The punditocracy on the BBC saw it, too. Former players Wayne Rooney and Joe Hart have been here before and treated this defeat much like revisiting a trauma. For the rest of us it was hard to miss: like staring into the face of the England team over the decades that have passed since 1966.

"The wait and the pain goes on for English football." 💔England's dream of reaching a first men's World Cup final since 1966 is over as Argentina make it six wins from six semi-final appearances 👏 pic.twitter.com/AEMHqqcYfI

Tuchel said that Argentina’s tactical changes as he saw them – two wide wingers, two central strikers – forced his hand. So too, he seemed to suggest, did the attitude of his players. He talked about them failing to be “active” as he called it, engaging their opposition and taking the game to them. But by this point those on the outside could see it more clearly than him.

This kind of retreat, to a greater or lesser degree, was the default position of so many England teams. England led against Brazil in 2002, Croatia in 2018, Italy in 2021. Sir Gareth Southgate, a man more criticised for a reluctance to make substitutions, never went into reverse quite as spectacularly as this. The record is now two World Cup semi-finals, and two European Championship finals in the last five tournaments. But that final step, or the penultimate one at the World Cup, is the primary English problem.

The recriminations from Atlanta will last for years, and as for the precious opportunity – who knows when it will come again?

Tuchel is part of this unfortunate history now, and defeats like this often suck reputations into the void. Afterwards he breezily turned over the page to Euro 2028, before England complete Saturday’s third-place play-off, although one feels that moving on will be more difficult than that.

After Fernández’s 85th-minute equaliser, Messi found the substitute Martínez at the back post for a winner seven minutes later. “There was blood in the water and we went for it,” Lionel Scaloni, the Argentina head coach, said. His team, to their credit, never gave up the chase.

They pursued that equaliser after Anthony Gordon’s 55th-minute goal, a fine finish after England launched a quick attack down the right that ended with Morgan Rogers sweeping the ball to the back post. England had just 12 per cent of the ball from that moment until Martínez’s 92nd-minute goal.

ENGLAND HAVE THE OPENER! 🤩Anthony Gordon puts the Three Lions ahead in the World Cup semi-final! pic.twitter.com/5fBlRcf1oI

This Argentina team are very hard to love, but you have to admire the tenacity with which they keep going. Around Messi is a fairly mixed bag of young talents and old boys clinging on. Their commitment to the cause, however, is not in doubt. They handle the moments of adversity better than most.

As for England, in the minutes that followed Gordon’s goal, Tuchel and his players seemed to make up their minds that what had sufficed for Norway and Mexico would work for Argentina.

He brought off Gordona after 72 minutes for Ezri Konsa and then Dan Burn and Nico O’Reilly came on for Reece James and Declan Rice. In the meantime, the game was following an inevitable path. There were nine attempts on the England goal, including the two that went in, after Gordon scored. Alexis Mac Allister somehow clipped a post with a header. Jordan Pickford made one of the saves of his life from the substitute Nicolás González. A post was struck again by Mac Allister before the second goal.

In other words: this goal was coming. This Argentina have some fine players, including Messi, Julián Alvarez, Fernández, Emiliano Martínez – but they are so much more than the sum of their parts. The game finished with the 38-year-old Nicolás Otamendi on the pitch. So too the MLS midfielder Rodrigo De Paul, as well as the right-back Gonzalo Montiel, 29, who did not make the grade on loan at Nottingham Forest.

“They were raised in an environment where they feared nothing,” Scaloni said of his players. “They don’t feel the weight on their shoulders.” In those painful last moments, Tuchel tried to reverse his earlier mistake by sending on Ivan Toney and Marcus Rashford, but the momentum had slipped away. England were beaten.

It had been intense from the start with the Argentine cynicism as high as ever. Elliot Anderson was targeted and eventually booked when Djed Spence nudged a charging Messi into the midfielder’s path. Spence was superb for much of the game, including a recovery tackle on Giuliano Simeone after the Gordon goal.

WHAT A TACKLE FROM DJED SPENCE 👊 pic.twitter.com/kyrHBS0tzX

At the critical moment when Messi prepared to cross for the Martínez goal, however, Spence seemed to feel a bolt of pain and could not react in time.

It was a gripping game, even without a single shot on target from either side in the first half. Ismail Elfath, the US referee for whom this game felt impossible at times, was slow to book Argentina players. They seemed to know who to target, in particular Jude Bellingham and Pickford. Bellingham had some fine moments in the first half but he struggled after the break.

England’s goal came 10 minutes after half-time, when the momentum had been with Argentina. Nicolás Tagliafico only just stopped Harry Kane’s long ball forward. From there Rice fed Rogers and the cross was perfect. At the back post, Gordon slipped past his man and guided it home, right-footed, at the back post.

In the aftermath England seemed to retreat. Tuchel said that he did not believe in a curse that afflicts England in the closing stages of such big knockout games. Of course, he was seeing it first hand for the first time – which, for the rest of us, is sadly not the case.

Thomas Müller: "I cannot believe and understand how England approached this game after they're leading. I cannot understand how they invited Argentina to play one cross after the other in perfect crossing positions" pic.twitter.com/Hm35pZfRwf

🚨 WATCH: Police rescue an Argentina fan in London after he was surrounded by England fans pic.twitter.com/ukDjubWuEV

[Reporter: Did the better team win?] “I don’t know. I thought we deserved to be 1-0 up. The momentum changed after that. They had nothing to lose and we suddenly played like we had a lot to lose. They took more and more risks and turned the game around in the last 20 minutes.

[Argentina had 88 per cent possession after Gordon’s goal] “It felt like that.” [What went wrong?] “We didn’t have enough possession to escape the pressure. We tried everything but couldn’t get hold of the ball. It’s like you’re dying a slow death. It started straight away after the goal and is the reason basically that we lost.”

“We were the better team until we cored then the mindset shifted, they took a lot of risks and have a lot of quality.

[You took Gordon off for Konsa at 71 minutes and sat deep] “We sat deep from when we scored the goal. Not after the substitutions. I take the responsibility. It’s easy to be a coach after the game. The result tells the story. No one can say what would have happened with other substitutions. I thought we needed a back five with all the crossing.

“We didn’t stop the second line coming through the gaps. We were not physical enough in these moments. It’s not about structure. You can play in any structure deep, you can defend in any structure if you’re active but we were too passive.

[Harry said he’d been here before, 1-0 up in the 2018 semi-final, 1-0 up in the Euro 2020 final] “I can’t speak about that I was not part of that.

“No regrets, we gave everything, that’s the bottom line. We gave everything. It’s difficult to accept because we hate to lose. We were very close. For the overall summary we have to wait a bit and digest it.

"I take the responsibility"Thomas Tuchel reacts as England's World Cup dream comes to an end following defeat to Argentina...🎙️ @gabrielclarke05 pic.twitter.com/Vrm071Zkd1

The FA extended Tuchel’s initial 18-month contract to the end of Euro 2028 last year. He was hired to be the ultimate “finisher”, focusing solely on the first team rather than all the other jobs as a figurehead for the elite pathway that Gareth Southgate filled. His job was specifically to get England over the line after two defeats in Euros finals, a World Cup semi and quarter.

Everyone deserves one tournament’s grace and he has gone farther than anyone bar Sir Alf, Sir Bobby and Sir Gareth. But when you talk so much about your players being brave, you also need to demonstrate your own courage. And clinging on for dear life, even if it worked in different circumstances against lesser opposition, is pusillanimous. Scaloni’s substitutions won the game for Argentina, Tuchel’s lost it for England.

Gutted. Tonight wasn't the result we all hoped for, but this England team has given it their all.The passion and energy they've shown representing the badge has made us all proud.

Gutted. England, you gave it everything and we are all so proud of you.Thank you to everyone on and off the pitch, for an incredible tournament. The fight and belief you have shown has inspired us all. The most complete England team in a tournament. Hold your heads high 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 W https://t.co/PDBNEsuVfS

12% - Average possession between Anthony Gordon's opener and Lautaro Martínez's winner (55th to 92nd minute):12% - 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 England88% - 🇦🇷 ArgentinaTrapped. pic.twitter.com/J5S9wlHCpx

2 - There are just two occasions of a team scoring first in the semi-final but not reaching the final of the FIFA World Cup in the 21st century – both of them are England (vs Croatia in 2018 and Argentina in 2026).Familiar. pic.twitter.com/X645w5FQLk

“We are disappointed. We got so close but we got too passive after we scored and conceded a lot of chances. We could not turn possession around and juts conceded so, so many chances, crosses and shots.

“We were so, so close but we couldn’t keep the level up after we scored.

“I also made offensive substitutions in the last games to try to help the players. We decided to go to a back five because the gaps were too large but they kept crossing and crossing. We went to a back five to close the gaps in the air and win headers. We concedes so many crosses and chances after our goal so we tried to help. But the responsibility is on the coach and if it doesn’t go well it is easy to say it is wrong.

“Yeah [we wanted to go for a second goal] but it doesn’t help when you can’t get the ball. I didn’t think an offensive substitution [at that point] would help. We got more and more passive. We couldn’t keep balls, we couldn’t win balls. It was not a structural problem after the goal. We changed nothing [in the immediate aftermath] but I understand these are the discussions and millions of coaches after the game know better.

“We can discuss this [whether they invited pressure] but I have to make a decision. I have to analyse what I see on the pitch and take responsibility.”

[Any regrets?] “Not at the moment. The team gave everything and we were very, very close. We deserved to be 1-0 up. We played one of our better matches, maybe the best match [of the tournament] but we couldn’t bring it over the line. No regrets.

[Did we ever see the Thomas Tuchel England you wanted to see?] “I don’t have an answer for that question. I don’t know what it means. I think we saw the mentality throughout the matches. We played strong teams in the group, a lot of miles, a lot of travelling, we played at altitude, with 10 men, in the heat and we were very, very close. It is not the time to analyse the tournament. We went very close but lost a crucial match.”

In the celebrations on the final whistle, Argentina fans threw on a banner proclaiming: “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” declaring that the Falkland Islands will remain theirs. This win will potentially renew their demands to claim the Falklands as their own.

We will see if Fifa applies its regulations and fines the AFA.

Tuchel played his hand. He wanted to hang on. We were hanging on against Norway and Mexico but they haven’t got the same quality as Argentina.

He played his cards very early and it’s backfired. We were all praising him in previous games, now we will go the other way. He could have put more pace on. The players were physically and mentally done once Argentina got that first goal.

“Gutted for the boys, everyone. The team, the staff, the fans. We played a good game for the majority of it. Once we went 1-0 up we tried to hold on but at this level you can’t.

“The lads have given everything. Running, sweat, blood tears, whatever. So to fall short like we did today is just gutting.

“We struggled to get pressure on the ball [after scoring]. Whether it was them putting more men forward or us not being able to match them man for man it was juts wave after wave. Lads were putting blocks in but it wasn’t enough.

“The boys are always ready. The message after we went ahead was to go and get another one but when they got their two goals we tried to find something but we couldn’t get back into it.

“We had a lot of good moments, good matches in this tournament. Another semi-final. We keep knocking on the door. We need to find that missing piece in the final part of the tournament. We’re just missing that final piece.”

Wayne Rooney: “We go one-nil up and we go five at the back, we go six at the back. If you allow Argentina to come on to you, you’re in trouble. We surrendered. If you let players of that quality have the ball, you’re in trouble.”

Joe Hart: “Gareth Southgate will be sat at home, watching, and he was criticised for big games when England had the lead, I don’t see anything has changed. For Thomas Tuchel… that’s him saying he didn’t believe in his team and couldn’t land any more punches on Argentina.”

Micah Richards: “Tactically we all thought he got it wrong with his changes.”

Tonight the changes didn’t work. Argentina deserved their victory. Sadly, it’s deja vu for England when the moment of truth arrived.

They froze after scoring. As Joe Hart says, they went back to what they did against Mexico and Norway and packed the defence but Argentina are not Norway or Mexico. They have an indomitable spirit, experience and some great players. You can sit back against Mexico and Norway. You can’t withstand a 30-minute siege against a team like Argentina.

England have lost a third World Cup semi-final. Argentina were the better team. They took more risks, made positive substitutions and found the attacking incisiveness that England lacked all game, apart from when setting up Gordon’s goal.

England pump a long ball up to Dan Burn and Argentina knock it clear. It has come to this.

Rashford gets to the byline on the left and cuts back a cross that Argentina clear. Then Bellingham brings down Messi and Montiel taunts Bellingham when the free-kick was awarded.

England are huffing and puffing, pumping long throws and crosses into the box but without the precision they need.

You can’t say Argentina have not deserved it for their response. They have shown why they are world champions.

I’m afraid England have been sitting ducks ever since they scored.

Rashford and Toney are on for Spence and Stones as England have a throw on the right.

England 1 Argentina 2 (Lautaro Martinez) Gonzalez slides a pass inside from the left to Mac Allister who flays a shot into the foot of the right post. Spence slides into knock it away from Messi but Messi races out to the right to retrieve it and arc over a right-foot cross that Lautaro Martinez creeps between Konsa and Stones to bury with a forceful header.

Lautaro Martinez wins it for Argentina in stoppage time 🇦🇷 pic.twitter.com/7DQKq2DIhk

Bellingham tries to relieve the siege with a long solo run up the left but can’t keep it going.

Nine minutes of stoppage time are signalled after Stones receives treatment for a head injury sustained in a collision with his keeper. He has to go off for a minute.

The chances were coming. Tuchel made his big decisions, but the crosses kept coming into the box. It’s not a great strike for me. The keeper has to save it. Now it’s an awkward one tactically. Tuchel will have to make another change.

England have been under the cosh for the past 20 minutes and have switched to a packed defence. Can they switch back and regain some momentum.

England have got four centre-backs on the pitch. Tuchel has to re-balance this. His changes to try to see the game out were understandable, although they ultimately haven’t worked. England will take extra-time at the moment, because Argentina have the momentum.

England 1 Argentina 1 (Fernandez) Messi takes the corner short to De Paul who gives it back to the captain. Messi then drills a pass to Enzo Fernandez 22 yards out, right of centre. He smashes a shot with his instep and, after four or five sighters, hits it with blistering power into the left of the goal.

What a goal from Enzo Fernandez for Argentina's equaliser 🎯 pic.twitter.com/R2mTZ98qBT

Pickford soars to his left to turn Fernandez’s shot over the bar.

This is a blow for Reece James and England. Has him hamstring gone again? We will find out for sure later, but here’s Big Dan Burn to try to get England over the line. Tuchel’s team have dropped very deep since going ahead and I’d worry about them finding a second wind if Argentina do manage to equalise.

O’Reilly and Burn come on for Rice and James. O’Reilly slots into midfield. Lautaro Martinez replaces Tagliafico.

Rogers mugs Messi in the tackle and bombs forward with Kane in tow but smacks his shot into a defender. Back come Argentina with a couple of crosses that force Anderson to head it off Mac Allister’s attempted bicycle klick and Kane to throw his body on the line to thwart Alvarez.

England are clinging on now and Messi clips a fantastic [ass with his left foot from the inside-right channel to the back post. Gonzalez peels off James and heads back across goal, looking for the far corner, but it drifts inches wide. Montiel drops to his haunches. Up goes the flag but it was mighty close and could have been overturned by VAR.

Moments later De Paul hammers an effort that Pickford saves low then gathers at the second attempt when Mac Allister was closing him down.

England are happy to soak up the pressure Argentina are trying to exert and attempt to hit them on the break but it’s nerve-racking.

De Paul’s swings in a cross with venomous whip and dip. Mac Allister gets up to head it powerfully into the heart of the left post. He had to score. Konsa picked the wrong man to mark.

England do go to five at the back with Konsa’s introduction for Gordon

Argentina send on De Paul, Otamendi and Montiel for Simeone, Molina and Lisandro Martinez.

Can England now stop Messi? This could be his last 25 minutes in international football and he is trying everything.

Argentina are coming. You can feel it as well as see it.

For then first time all day, Buenos Aires fell silent as Anthony Gordon put England in front.

Pickford saves England’s lead with a one-handed, scooped save from Gonzalez’s header, the sub artfully picked out by Messi’s cross. Is it too soon for Dan Burn and five at the back?

Fine pass from Kane opens up Argentina on England’s right and James feeds a pass across the 18-yard line to Rice. His attempted daisycutter of a shot turns into a pea-roller and is an easy save for Emi Martinez.

Stones stops the substitute’s first touch, a header back across goal, from reaching Alvarez with a crucial header.

Fernandez fires a shot over the bar after Argentina’s most sustained spell of possession of the match.

Even Victoria Beckham was up celebrating that England goal. She’d stayed in her seat against Norway, but was up hugging husband David when Gordon’s shot at the back post hit the back of the net.

Colossal sense of catharsis as Anthony Gordon, the calmest man in the building, propels England towards the World Cup final with an almost nonchalant finish from Morgan Rogers’ exquisite cross.

Argentina do not panic when behind and have started to play with more fluency as England let them have the ball. Kane shows remarkable composure in his own box to shield the ball from two attackers and see it into safe harbour.

The two wingers combine brilliantly! How long have we wanted more England attackers to come to the party in this World Cup? England needed something else tonight and they’ve got it big style.

Argentina were on the verge of equalising when a mistake allows Simeone to storm down the right and into the box. Just as he was about to pull the trigger on a shot, Spence hared back to slide in and knock the ball behind for a corner. Amazing.

WHAT A TACKLE FROM DJED SPENCE 👊 pic.twitter.com/kyrHBS0tzX

England 1 Argentina 0 (Gordon) Kane chips a 25-yard pass from the centre looking for Rogers down the right. Tagliafico hooks it back upfield straight to Rice who finds Rogers. The Villa forward gallops down the wing then bends over a superb cross. Gordon diddles Molina by coming found the blindside to steer in a volley.

ENGLAND HAVE THE OPENER! 🤩Anthony Gordon puts the Three Lions ahead in the World Cup semi-final! pic.twitter.com/5fBlRcf1oI

That was a superb England move from the moment Tagliafico made a mess of clearing Kane’s long ball. Gordon’s finish right in the money. It was always going to have to be good. Let’s see how Argentina respond.

Molina’s cross from the right is ripe with menace but England see it off.

The two sides of Romero, an amazingly insouciant touch in the box a split-second before Gordon as about to steal the ball off him and a turn away from fanger. Then, moments later, he grabs Bellingham round the waist to stop him driving past and is belatedly booked.

England defend the corner taken by Messi short so that he can be played back in up the byline. Bellingham stands his ground and Messi cannot wriggle past him, finding only the brick wall of Bellingham’s torso.

That’s how to deal with Messi. Body in the way first, keep contact, steer him away from trouble. Superb from Bellingham.

Emi Martinez dwells on the ball, trying to invite the press. England stand off and eventually the keeper launches it. Simeone beats Guehi to flick it on and Alvarez drives past Spence and then shoots towards the near post. Pickford gets down low to beat it away.  Alvarez beats Spence to the rebound and has another go, smashing it into the side netting via a faint deflection.

The biggest cheer of the half here in the Fan Fest arena at the Palermo came when Messi was fouled by Elliot Anderson, prompting the 10,000 fans here to jump up and down to let no-one in doubt that they are English. Otherwise, it has been fairly muted. Perhaps they have been a bit embarrassed about the lack of cards. It suggests England are so far holding their own.

Rice, with one leg of his shorts hitched up, kicks off. No changes. The referee insists the kick-off be taken again as Anthony Gordon had crossed the line before the whistle. Pickford pumps a 70-yard pass up the middle, looking for Kane. Romero wins the header.

We wanted to be the aggressor, we wanted to be on the front foot and get after them – to show there was no inferiority complex and that we’re here to play in their half.

I think it worked until the water break. After that it was a bit more difficult for us to get the ball – they dropped Messi and Enzo [Fernandez] outside our block and got some possession. But it’s still absolutely OK, and the evolution for us is to take this dominance and turn it into bigger chances.

The more time we spend in their half, the more tired they’ll get.

A cagey half, which is to be expected given the stakes. I’ve been impressed with England. They’ve looked dangerous without creating any clear chances. Argentina have created nothing so far.

What’s encouraging is England look like they belong out there, going head-to-head with the world champions, and Elliot Anderson has been outstanding.

This has been the opposite of what the rest of the tournament has been for us. In previous matches there have been a lot of average performances and our two best players have shone. This time, England have played well as a collective while the two best players have been quiet. Bellingham and Kane might have their moment in the second half.

Too many fouls, too many stoppages by design. No shots on target. Both teams are scrapping but there has been very little quality. The foul count is 19, seven by England, 12 by Argentina.

Three shots on goal, none of them on target, just about sums up that first half. Both sides have had a player booked and Kane, Messi and Bellingham have all gone to the referee at the break. This has been scrappy and ill-tempered, but also pretty absorbing.

England work the free-kick to Gordon whose cross is deflected over the bar for a corner but the referee blows for half-time before it can be taken. Clive Thomas, at the age of 90, nods approvingly.

The signal goes up for three minutes of stoppage time, the absolute minimum.

Paredes is penalised for dangerous play for raising his studs in a challenge on James.

It is compelling to watch but not particularly elevating. Romero makes a good tackle on Bellingham. When he is in control of his emotions, he is a fine defender.

England have not made much from their dozen free-kicks. More haste less speed.

The referee sees Lisandro Martinez pulling Rogers’ shirt and finally acts.

FINALLY, this referee has remembered he can also book the players in the navy blue. Lisandro Martinez: yellow.

It’s become cat-and-mouse with Argentina getting more of the ball in the last ten minutes. The one worry is Messi is just starting to take possession much more with some great touches. He hasn’t hurt England yet, though. The hydration break stopped some momentum again, but Tuchel will be pleased overall so far.

Argentina defend the free-kick staunchly as Anderson cannot get above Tagliafico then Messi breaks, hangs on to the ball with sumptuous skill, beating Kane, Spence and Rice before Anderson launches himself at the No10 to stop him. Argentina surround the referee with the distaste of someone who had heard a guest break wind in front of the King. Eventually they get on with the free-kick. Messi tries to dribble straight down the middle, can’t do so but the ball breaks to Fernandez who fires a shot that scratches the top of the cross-bar. That was alarmingly close.

Close for Argentina!Enzo Fernandez fires a rocket of a strike that flies just over the bar 🚀 pic.twitter.com/WMeSkTajtQ

Great piece of skill from Messi. Incredible strength to hold off Kane. Spence nudged Messi into Anderson but it’s always a nightmare when Messi is facing goal and running like that.

Simeone gets away with a foul on Guehi without a booking when he shoves the centre-forward up the jacksie. England attack down the left with Gordon beating his man before being thwarted by Lisandro Martinez’s recovery tackle. Spence pounces on the loose ball and to stop England Molina makes a daft foul on Bellingham.

Rice takes the free-kick from the left, whipping it with his right to the far post where Stones cranes his neck but was too tightly marked by Lisandro Martinez to work it towards goal.

Paredes spots Molina’s lung-bursting 70-yard run down the right but overhits his diagonal. England take the goal-kick short then work it up to Bellingham who is brought down 25 yards from goal, quite deliberately by a combination of Romero and Fernandez.

Romero next foul is surely a booking. That foul on Bellingham would have been a yellow in the Premier League

James is penalised for a foul on Mac Allister down the right which looked like a foul on the England right-back. Tuchel auditions for the Ministry of Silly Walks in his foot-stomping ire on the touchline.

Pickford scuffs a left-foot clearance and Alvarez is well positioned to pounce on it but he miscontrols his pass to Messi who responds in kind.

First hydration break. No doubt Argentina are trying to wind England up. Noticeable and positive that both Rice and Bellingham have responded by laughing at their tormentors. Eleven fouls in 24 minutes.

There wasn’t an awful lot of football in that first quarter of the game. It’s just been very, very scrappy. Neither set of players seem particularly happy with the referee, which probably tells you he’s done a decent job so far.

Spence stays tight to Simeone after an Argentina free-kick is taken short. The left-back closes the gap and the cross rebounds off his shins for a corner. Pickford tries to push Simeone away as they wait for the corner as the winger tries to block him. The ref tells them to stop messing around and then blows once the corner is launched as Simeone wrapped his arms around the keeper.

After a couple of decent thrusts down the left, England’s right flank gets weaving with Rogers finding the overlapping James whose cross is smothered by Argentina.

The referee Ismail Elfath is really being tested in these early stages. Chiefly by Argentina. Paredes is after Bellingham. Every challenge on Messi is claimed as a foul by Argentina.

It’s clear this is going to be a huge test of the England players’ ability to concentrate on their plan, and to not get drawn into the emotion of the game. On top of that, Argentina are a good side and they are probing for weaknesses. They have come out very aggressively.

England have started well. They look confident and dangerous – more than Argentina. Argentina want to make this a dark arts game. They are better than us at that ‘nasty’ stuff. We can’t get involved in any of that.

Wonderful tackle by Paredes on Bellingham instigates an Argentina counter during which Messi claims he was fouled. He wasn’t but that doesn’t stop him waving his arms around in exasperation. England try to attack up the left only to be stopped by a foul on Gordon. From the quickly taken free-kick, Spence makes great headway down the left, beating Molina again only for Fernandez to race back and force him off the ball and into touch.

Somebody is going to boil over here. Paredes and Fernandez are constantly looking to goad England’s players, much to the chagrin of Thomas Tuchel and captain Harry Kane, who seems to be urging US referee Ismail Elfath to take closer control.

Excellent combination between Gordon and Spence down the England left gets the better of Molina. He cuts in, takes a touch too many which takes him into five Argentina defenders who swarm round him with recovery runs. Sheer weight of numbers push him back.

A foul on Rogers ends with a drop ball after Anderson was deemed to have hurt Paredes in a firm but not illegal tackle. The ref is going to have to get a card out soon. Tuchel is going garrity with Scaloni and the level of diving by Argentina. The most naked example of that is when Simeone picks up the ball having been caught offside and Pickford bumps him as he tries to get it back. Simeone goes down as if kneecapped.

Gordon chases a long pass down the left that has too much on it but he gets there in the nick of time but can’t find Rogers’ run down the inside-left channel. Emi Martinez gathers.

Anderson buys a third free-kick off Simeone with excellent positioning but, after Kane is tackled by Paredes, he fouls Fernandez in this tit for tat start.

Rogers drives at Tagliafico, reaches the byline and whips over a cross that Argentina head behind for a corner. Rice goes long. Simeone wrestles Stones over but the referee waves play on until a high boot clips Messi.

Spence makes good progress down the left, riding a tackle before a forceful sliding tackle wins the ball back. England regroup and Simeone fouls Anderson .

Bellingham and Paredes were mouthing off at each other after that Fernandez foul on Anderson. Messi then had a go at Bellingham too. Feisty start!

England continue to press high and there’s a stand-off between the players with the gobby Paredes in Bellingham’s face after Messi is not given a free-kick when Anderson holds his shoulder. Fernandez retaliates with a chop down Anderson’s shin. Messi, trying to referee the game, gets up in the referee’s grill.

Argentine fans drown out the God Save The King with their own song. England fans respond in kind with the Argentinian anthem. This is a real World Cup knockout tie - and nothing even the stadium address system can do about it. It’s electric in the stadium. I was in Dallas yesterday for the first semi-final and the mood was nothing like as fierce as this.

Argentina kick off, attacking from right to left. Messi, alone in the centre-circle, rolls it to Paredes who works it all the way back to Emi Martinez. England press high and force a throw-in.

England give the ball to the centre-backs who sweep it across the back four. Mac Allister tries to disrupt the spell of possession with a shove.

Michael Buffer’s “champions of the worrrrrrld” billing for England feels a touch generous given it was 60 years ago. I have watched him perform his master of ceremonies shtick in several sports and he barely changes a word. Still, it has earned him, at a conservative estimate, £300m.

God Save the King goes first and is resoundingly booed by the Argentina fans. England supporters respond by whistling and jeering through Himno Nacional Argentino.

Chelsea co-owner Todd Boehly is inside the Atlanta stadium and has picked his side... Chelsea vice-captain Enzo Fernandez might not be too happy.

Todd Boehly 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 pic.twitter.com/whiQnVJkNs

A reminder that England will play in all white, Argentina in navy shirts with black shorts and socks.

Benedict gives us a talking to, ASMR style, over a montage, ending with ‘Are you ready?’

A sign? American TV is making a thing of how the England team bus overtook the Argentina team bus, which was snarled up in traffic, on its way to the stadium earlier. Looks like they found a quicker route.

England fans are certainly outnumbered inside the Atlanta stadium, with pockets of Argentina fans in among the main England sections. It has all seem good-natured so far, so let’s hope that lasts.

Pleased to report that Sir Mick Jagger is here and singing along to ‘Sweet Caroline’. TV cameras have located him.

Reporters from all countries sitting together. I’m assuming my neighbour is Argentine judging by the maté and Lionel Messi flask.

Governor of the Falkland Islands, Colin Martin-Reynolds lights up Government House with the colours of the England flag.

Once we had the draw, we knew the possible way, these are the games that you dream of to get to where you’re trying to reach, not only reach, don’t forget, but win.

They are specialists [full-backs] and deserve to play. Reece has the quality to play at the very highest level and shows no nerves. The speed of Djed, and he was very good in the last two games from the bench, and I think we need to get our full-backs forward to protect. That’s why.

It’s just a feeling, a stomach feeling from the coach about Morgan. He has something special tp give today. He was very good in the last game against Norway and had an outstanding training session to follow up on that performance.

You need a lot of keys [to contain Messi], a complete performance offensively and defensively to stop the supply to Messi, to stop his support and his runs on our right side when he gest the ball and turns. We need to play with freedom, also for the mindset, we should be ready for the fight, calm and collected to give them some problems to solve. We’re up for it.

Lionel Scaloni has given a nod to the historic rivalry of this fixture by picking Diego Simeone’s son in his starting line-up. Giuliano Simeone is given his first appearance since the final group stage match against Jordan, when Argentina had already sealed a place in the knockouts. His father was famously on the end of David Beckham’s boot 28 years ago in Saint-Étienne. This just adds to the feeling there will be some flashpoint in the next few hours in Atlanta.

While Thomas Tuchel has changed his backline, Argentina are playing the same back four from the team that defeated Switzerland. Simeone is the only change, coming in for Rodrigo De Paul. This could mean a change of system for the world champions – if Enzo Fernández drifts to the right, they could look very 4-4-2.

It doesn’t get much bigger, the biggest competition in football against the holders.

We know what Argentina are about. We’ve got a game plan we’re ready to set up against.

The manager’s made a decision. Morgan is an incredible player, he’s fast, strong and can come inside. He’s a player we’re all looking forward to playing with.

I’m back to normal. I’m 100 per cent, fully refreshed and ready to go.

The team will shock a few people because of Djed Spence’s inclusion. What I like about Thomas Tuchel’s approach is that keeping the same team would be a much easier decision, particularly in a game of this magnitude.

The manager is consistent in selecting players for specialist roles. Just as he called up Dan Burn in case England needed to revert to a back five (as they did against Mexico), the reason he likes Spence is for situations requiring one-on-one defending. Tuchel clearly believes Spence’s pace is a vital attribute in this situation, even if facing Lionel Messi is the ultimate challenge. This is the whole point of Spence being in the squad. If England win, the same logic would suggest he would be asked to mark Lamine Yamal in the final.

From that perspective, maybe we should not be so shocked by the choice.

Morgan Rogers comes in because Tuchel simply could not go with Madueke again. He was poor against Norway, and Saka has not looked fully fit all tournament. Saka is still a good option from the bench.

Overall, Rogers has played well whenever he’s been given a chance, so he’s gone with the man showing form.

This is the first game where England are playing a team who will expect to have as much of, if not more, of the ball than us. Every other game has followed the same pattern, certainly at the start, where England were considered the higher level team and tried to go after the opponent.

That’s not necessarily going to be the case here because we are clearly not favourites, and Argentina will look to apply all the early pressure. Argentina have the edge coming into the match because they are a team that has shown in recent international tournaments that they know how to get over the line.

England deserve to be at this stage, but the question remains: do we have the capacity to do what is habitual for nations like Argentina – finding a way when it matters most in the latter stages of a World Cup?

This is a night for bravery, which means getting on the ball and controlling the game. That could be achieved against every other opponent in this tournament so far, even if some of the victories have been flawed. Doing so against Argentina requires another layer of courage.

England (Pickford; James, Stones, Guehi, Spence; Anderson, Rice; Rogers, Bellingham, Gordon; Kane.Substitutes Trafford, D Henderson, O’Reilly, Konsa, Saka, Rashford, Chalobah, Burn, Mainoo, Watkins, Madueke, Eze, Toney.

Argentina E Martínez; Molina, Romero, Lisandro Martínez, Tagliafico; Paredes; Simeone, Fernández, Mac Allister; Messi, Alvárez.Substitutes  Musso, Rulli, Senesi, Montiel, Barco, Lo Celso, Palacios, González, Almada, De Paul, Paz, Otamendi, López, Lautaro Martínez, Medina.

Britain’s ambassador to the United States has urged England fans to remain on their best behaviour as tensions mount ahead of the World Cup semi-final against Argentina.

Sir Christian Turner called on travelling supporters in Atlanta to continue to act as “ambassadors for the country” amid fears that the historic dispute over the Falkland Islands could spill into violence.

The FBI has designated Wednesday night’s match “high risk”, making it the most serious security concern of the tournament so far.

“Continue to support each other, whatever the outcome,” Sir Chris told The Telegraph. “Enjoy the moment, enjoy the occasion, enjoy the hospitality. It’s a game of football.”

Tensions have been inflamed by recent claims from the Argentine government that Britain is an “usurping” power and that the Falkland Islanders were “artificially implanted”.

So far, England’s games in the tournament have seen little to no violence.

Of the estimated 50,000 fans who have made the journey to the United States for the World Cup, just 25 needed assistance from the embassy for issues like lost passports, medical problems, or visa help.

“It’s a wonderful sign of how the fans have been ambassadors for the country,” Sir Chris added.

Thomas Tuchel has twice picked Jude Bellingham and Morgan Rogers in the same starting line-up. In the group stages against Panama, Bellingham had a deeper role in midfield and Rogers was the No10. The only other time they have started was Tuchel’s second match in charge, when he fielded the childhood pals in the win over Latvia.

Tuchel has never picked a back four of Reece James, John Stones, Marc Guéhi and Djed Spence during his time in charge of England.

John Byers is – and I’m sure he won’t mind me saying it – one of the older England fans at this World Cup. He’s 68 now and was eight when England won the thing. He remembers it well. He made a banner out of toilet paper, grabbed his mum’s red lipstick and scrawled E-N-G-L-A-N-D on it, a letter on each piece of loo roll. “This is our best chance to beat Argentina,” he says, “They haven’t been too good so far. We’ve got the better team.”

John, who worked in construction, retired four weeks ago especially in time for the World Cup. He’s from Birmingham and used to go and see Jude Bellingham playing in the Birmingham City youth team. “ I watched Jude as a nine-year-old and I used to tell everybody this guy is a diamond. I was right.”

Morgan Rogers deserves his chance for England and it makes sense to use him on the right, behind Harry Kane, which has become a problem position with Bukayo Saka not fully fit and Noni Madueke struggling. Rogers has made an impact from the bench and also did well when he started against Panama. Crucially he is also fairly fresh and raring to go. Feels like it could be a big game ahead for him alongside his friend, Jude Bellingham.

Giuliano Simeone, the youngest of El Cholo, Diego Simeone’s three footballing sons, replaces Rodrigo De Paul on the right of midfield:

Argentina  E Martínez; Molina, Romero, Lis Martínez, Tagliafico; Paredes; Simeone, E Fernández, Mac Allister; Messi, Alvárez.

And there are three changes flagged earlier:

Rogers replaces Saka, Spence is in for O’Reilly and James takes Konsa’s place.

Ready for Argentina! 👊 pic.twitter.com/5fSh9K1tir

You wonder why Messi even needs an accreditation lanyard. As he enters the stadium, most of the security staff simply stop to take pictures of him.

Just In: England players are now on their way to Atlanta Stadium. The countdown to the semi-final is officially ON. 🏟️ pic.twitter.com/tJxUME3i1v

England players are on the pitch, having a look at the surface and taking in the atmosphere. Plenty of jeers as they head back to the dressing room – and big cheers when Argentina’s coach arrives at Atlanta Stadium.

Traffic jams across Buenos Aires as the city gathers to watch the game. No doubt about the result here.

Birmingham Moor Street Station has been renamed Bellingham Moor Street ahead of England's World Cup semi-final. Chiltern Railways is showing its support ahead of the crucial clash with Argentina tonight. The new sign can be seen on Platform 3. pic.twitter.com/E9ASXmQozj

Reece James is an excellent full-back, offering more than Ezri Konsa, a centre-half, in terms of crossing ability and as an accomplished midfielder, he is comfortable moving into the inside-right channel. Nico O’Reilly usually does that job on the left and maybe Tuchel is sacrificing his ability to ghost into attacking positions for Spence’s thrust and greater tackling?  As for Rogers, Saka is not fit to play much more than an hour and Tuchel obviously thinks he is better used against a tiring defence than using him to set the tone.

Rogers often plays wide for Villa and, although he will not drive to the byline as often as Madueke, his delivery will be more reliable.

It’s all been super good natured in and around the stadium. So far at least. Not least because there are just tens of thousands of Argentinian fans, hugely outnumbering England supporters. We’ll see what it’s like at kick-off inside the stadium but I expect this to be another England away game. And we did OK in the Azteca in Mexico with the crowd against us.

Officials tell me that they anticipate – or at least are most worried – if Argentina lose. While England’s animus is sporting (Hand of God in 1986 and the Beckham kick in 1998), theirs is political. Obviously the vast majority of fans on both sides are fantastically well-behaved but there are big worries from a security point of view if Argentina go out today.

The skies are grey over Buenos Aires, but the city is already resplendent in La Albiceleste colours.

Dawn was just breaking this morning when I spotted a homeless gentleman walking along the walkway beside the docks in Puerto Madero wearing an Argentina top.

The lady serving in the bakery near Plaza de Mayo, where the official seat of government is located in Casa Rosada (the Pink House), was wearing her football top under work clothes, so she could make a quick get-away to the official fan festival in the Palermo district.

By mid-morning, the city was a sea of white and sky blue. In contrast, I have seen just one England supporter brave enough to don his football jersey and even he was having second thoughts about keeping it on.

Mike McGrath stole this from some Argentina fans in our hotel lobby – it’s coming home! Or he is….

Ian Wright has attracted criticism from Falklands veterans after predicting England’s World Cup semi-final against Argentina will be a “war”.

The former Arsenal and England striker was previewing tonight’s tie as part of ITV’s coverage of Spain’s victory over France on Tuesday evening.

“There’s going to be chaos in the game; there’s going to be chaos in the stands; they’re not separating the fans. It’s a game where we’re going to have to show a lot of composure,” said Wright, who won 33 caps for England.

“It’s a country that, as time’s gone by, I’ve learnt a lot about them, and I have no love for them. Obviously, [Diego] Maradona’s somebody that’s done some amazing things I’ve seen.

“It’s a team that we have to beat and it’s going to be a tough one; it’s going to be a real tough one, a real attritional war we’re going into, and we have to recognise that.

“I’ve heard Thomas Tuchel saying it’s just a game. It’s not just a game, and they’ll realise it’s not just a game. It’s going to be more than that when they play.”

255 British soldiers lost their lives during the 1982 Falklands War. Simon Weston, who suffered severe burns during the Argentine bombing of the Galahad Ship, condemned the comparison between a football match and war.

“Some people describe a footballer as a hero on the field but that’s completely misusing the language,” he told The Telegraph. “They’re footballers. It’s hardly like they’re risking their lives on the pitch. It’s nothing like a battlefield.”

Marc Guéhi has claimed there is “no pressure at all” on England ahead of their semi-final against Argentina.

The England centre-back said the onus was on Argentina to win the game as World Cup holders.

“What’s the pressure? The onus is on them, they are the world champions,” Guéhi said.

“They need to come out and defend their title so there is no pressure on us at all.”

🗣️ "What's the pressure? The onus is on them. They're the world champions. They need to come out and defend their title."England defender Marc Guehi says the pressure is on Argentina ahead of the World Cup semi-final 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 pic.twitter.com/Ffu3YAojyD

The Manchester City defender was a second-half substitute in England’s tournament opener against Croatia but has started every game since then, including the entirety of the extra-time victory over Norway in the previous round.

“Both sides have big players. When you have that, you know it’s going to be a good game. It’s going to be a fun watch,” he added.

“It’s one you’re going to be talking about for a long time, so we’re excited.”

Remarkable flag-waving scenes in Atlanta, where Argentina fans have been making their presence felt...

BANDERAZO ARGENTINO EN ATLANTA 🇦🇷@Quilmes_Cerveza 🍻 pic.twitter.com/lLygS7ybAp

England’s rugby players will resist the temptation to wear their national team training kit out in public in Buenos Aires in the build-up to their Nations Championship Test against Argentina on Saturday.

Steve Borthwick’s side are scheduled to arrive in the Argentine capital on Thursday and are braced for a hostile reception should their footballing counterparts reach the World Cup final with victory in Atlanta this evening.

Alex Coles, the England second row, said: “I think, bearing in mind where we are and who we’re playing with, we’ve been pretty sensible about not wearing our English shirts around too much.”

Tommy Freeman, Coles’s England and Northampton team-mate, added: “We’ll see how hostile it gets. It’s big for Argentina and us and being here it’s heightened massively.”

1 - Tonight is 🇦🇷 Lionel Messi's first ever match against England.In the UEFA Champions League, Messi faced English teams 36 times and was involved in 33 goals (27 goals, 6 assists), a record for a player against clubs of one nation.Acquainted. pic.twitter.com/HUnhFpZYvb

Thomas Tuchel has produced a reassuringly indifferent response to the news that Argentina will wear their “lucky” kit tonight.

The holders will swap their traditional sky blue and white stripes for their navy blue away strip. England, as the designated home side in the tie, will wear their all-white home kit.

Argentina previously wore dark blue in World Cup victories over the English in 1986, when Diego Maradona scored his infamous “Hand of God” goal, and again in 1998, when England were eliminated on penalties in the round of 16.

“I would have done the same if there ⁠was any superstition combined with it,” said Tuchel. “So credit to them. I was not aware of that.”

The German also admitted he had his own superstitions which help him manage stress level before a big game.

“I have my superstitious routines. ​I will not tell you because another superstition ‌is that if I tell you, it will not work,” he said.

“We have routines that keep you grounded and calm through the day, and that will not change. We have, of course, also ‌our ​lucky charms, and these things ⁠are just normal in high-level sport.”

"I would have done the same." 😅Thomas Tuchel is asked about claims that Argentina are wearing their 'lucky' blue shirt against England 🤔 pic.twitter.com/GkjPQqBsAd

22 - England have lost none of their last 22 games against nations beginning with the letter A and have only conceded one goal in their last 17 against A-teams.Sheeran. https://t.co/f8L42u7k3Y pic.twitter.com/86GH2dvWZ4

Sir Keir Starmer has used his final appearance at Prime Minister’s Questions to wish England well in tonight’s World Cup semi-final.

Having been compared to Jude Bellingham by Graham Stewart, the Conservative MP for Beverley and Holderness, Starmer told the House of Commons: “For the England team, as with my successor [Andy Burnham], I won’t give advice, I will simply give my wholehearted support.

“And Mr Speaker, just for the record, I don’t care what the score is tonight as long as we win.”

🚨 WATCH: Keir Starmer jokes about tonight's England vs Argentina match in his final PMQs "This morning I had meetings with Ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this House, I have an important appointment with the television at 8pm" #PMQs pic.twitter.com/UVP7n8dpTY

We’re still around five hours from any official announcement on team news, but the early indications are that Thomas Tuchel is considering retaining the back line that started England’s extra-time victory over Norway.

Tuchel deployed a back four containing Ezri Konsa, John Stones, Marc Guehi and Nico O’Reilly in the previous round before introducing Reece James, Djed Spence and Dan Burn off the bench.

James, the Chelsea right-back, is available to start from the off in Atlanta after recovering from a hamstring injury he picked up in the goalless draw with Ghana.

Tuchel opted to field Konsa at right-back in the absence of James and the suspended Jarell Quansah and could stick with the Aston Villa defender after impressing against Erling Haaland and Co.

Elsewhere, Declan Rice is likely to keep his starting place in midfield. The Arsenal midfielder was withdrawn at half-time against Norway after being struck down with a stomach bug in the build-up to the game but has sufficiently recovered to be considered for selection this evening.

The other dilemma facing Tuchel is who to start on the right side of attack. Bukayo Saka impressed after replacing Noni Madueke against Norway, but there have been previous concerns over a chronic Achilles issue.

Tuchel also has the option of bringing in Marcus Rashford and playing him on the right or switching Anthony Gordon from the left. Morgan Rogers, the Aston Villa playmaker is another option on the right side of attack after he made an impressive contribution off the bench in the quarter-finals.

Sam Wallace, Telegraph Sport’s chief football writer, summaries the significance of tonight’s tie and explains why it could represent Lionel Messi’s final game in international football.

📅 1962, 1966, 1986, 1998, 2002... now, 2026.Tomorrow's semi-final will mark the sixth time England has faced Argentina at a World Cup.The Three Lions beat their South American foes three out of those five times. Can Tuchel's squad win a fourth match?@SamWallaceTel breaks… pic.twitter.com/fx0tbjgGdl

Wayne Rooney, the former England forward, has made another outlandish claim which I hope doesn’t come back to bite him.

Less than a week after he promised to row down the River Mersey if Norway beat Brazil to reach the World Cup quarter-finals, Rooney has made an equally bullish prediction for tonight’s semi-final...

"If Harry Kane is on it, he'll destroy these two centre-backs" 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🇦🇷 pic.twitter.com/9vqdSouHMJ

Police in Atlanta, Georgia, have been forced to intervene after rival sets of Argentina fans were involved in violent clashes on the eve of tonight’s semi-final.

Glass bottles, tables and chairs were thrown in an incident involving supporters of Argentine clubs San Lorenzo and Huracan.

Argentina supporters were asked to gather for a “flag-waving rally” the night before their nation’s last-four tie against England but the event descended into chaos when two ultra groups started fighting and caused many to flee for their safety.

With a place in the World Cup final on the line, Argentina supporters are resorting to bizarre methods in a bid to curse England’s hopes of progressing.

One fan told Reuters: “During this World Cup, when my friends and I get get together, we freeze the players. We put the star player and the goalkeeper on the same piece of paper and freeze in it in the freezer.”

⚽ Argentina fans in Buenos Aires perform pre-match rituals such as freezing stickers of rival players and wearing lucky jerseys ahead of the World Cup semi-final against England https://t.co/HcoxGvDyvH pic.twitter.com/YncKZOupLS

For those requiring a detailed history on the acrimony at the heart of this storied rivalry, look no further than Sam Wallace’s excellent essay, which explains why this tie will always be more than just a football match.

Here’s a snippet of Sam on the fixture’s most infamous chapter: the 1986 World Cup quarter-final, which took place four years after the Falklands War.

“You can’t grasp what it all means to the people back home, but something tells you it is the greatest experience you will have as a player.” Gary Lineker, with a hat-trick against Poland and two more goals in the last-16 win over Paraguay, had assessed the mood correctly before England’s match against Argentina at the Estadio Azteca. But even he could not have guessed what was to come.

The war between Britain and Argentina, just four years earlier, hung heavily over the game. “I am a football manager, not a politician,” Bobby Robson, the England manager, said: “Don’t ask me that sort of question.”

Midfielder Glenn Hoddle warned that Maradona had learned from his experiences at the 1982 World Cup and “really come on strong”. He pondered whether England should man-mark Maradona and suggested left-back Kenny Sansom. “I don’t think we should change the way we play because of him,” Hoddle said. “You would have to re-shape the whole side.”

The Argentine players gave each of the England team a present before the game. Maradona punched the ball into the England goal in the 51st minute. His brilliant second was four minutes later. Lineker scored his sixth of the tournament and England lost 2-1.

In just over 10 hours time we will know the identity of Spain’s World Cup final opponents after the European champions dispatched 2018 winners and pre-tournament favourites France on Tuesday evening.

Immortality beckons for England, who are braced for their biggest match in a generation with familiar foes Argentina standing between them and a first World Cup final since 1966.

This is a fixture steeped in history. The two nations are meeting at a World Cup for the sixth time, renewing a bitter rivalry that has produced some of the tournament’s most memorable moments and enduring controversies.

Thomas Tuchel’s side have reached the last four without being entirely convincing. They needed extra time to beat Norway in the quarter-finals after surviving for over half an hour with 10 men against co-hosts Mexico in the previous round.

England’s fortunes have been intrinsically linked to the performances of Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham, who have scored six goals apiece to keep Tuchel’s side alive at this tournament.

Argentina’s route to the latter stages has been just as arduous. The defending champions needed extra time to overcome both Cape Verde and Switzerland, while they came from 2-0 down with 11 minutes remaining to beat Egypt and avoid one of the biggest shocks in World Cup history.

The holders remain on course to become only the third side after Italy (1934, 1938) and Brazil (1958, 1962) to retain their crown and in the process give Lionel Messi the fairy-tale end to a remarkable international career.

The 39-year-old has scored eight goals in the tournament and remains central to everything to Argentina’s fortunes. Remarkably, despite a career spanning more than two decades, tonight’s semi-final meeting will be Messi’s first ever international appearance against England.

Tuchel has spoken openly about the scale of the challenge facing his players. Stopping Messi has become one of football’s great unsolved problems, but the 52-year-old German insists his team must focus on imposing their own game plan rather than being consumed with the

Rarely has so much been at stake for both nations. For England, it is another chance to move one step closer to ending a wait that has now stretched almost 60 years. For Argentina, it is an opportunity to go level with Italy and Germany for the second-most World Cup titles (four). Either way, one of football’s most storied rivalries is about to add another chapter.

#2057. Report: Liverpool increasingly likely to sanction January exit for player in ‘agonising’ situation

One Liverpool player seems increasingly likely to leave Anfield in January as his situation on Merseyside becomes ‘increasingly agonising’.

Having struggled for starts in two seasons under Arne Slot, Federico Chiesa would no doubt have been hoping that a change of head coach might’ve provided the springboard towards an increase in game-time.

Instead, the 29-year-old’s standing at LFC has diminished even further, having played just two minutes under Andoni Iraola so far despite recovering from a back injury almost a month ago.

According to Dean Jones for Flashscore, a January exit from Liverpool for the forward seems ‘increasingly possible’, and a return to his native Italy ‘could provide an attractive solution’ for both player and club.

Lazio, Inter Milan and Roma have been touted as clubs who ‘could explore the possibility’ of bringing Chiesa back to Serie A after he left Juventus for the Reds in 2024, although any such move would depend on what kind of deal the Merseysiders are prepared to consider.

The report adds that the 29-year-old’s situation ‘is becoming increasingly agonising’ as he continues to struggle for game-time at Anfield.

Want more Empire of the Kop coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

That Chiesa didn’t even make the substitutes’ bench against Arsenal on Sunday despite being fit and available is a damning indictment of where he stands in the pecking order.

The additions of Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola over the summer added further competition for places in the forward line, and the form of Lewis Koumas has seen him leap ahead of the Italian in the queue.

Iraola had six forwards either as starters or substitutes at the weekend, and he still has Hugo Ekitike to return from injury, so Chiesa is effectively our eighth-choice attacker.

His status at Liverpool was summed up a few weeks ago by Roy Keane’s throwaway comment of ‘Is he still there?‘ when the 29-year-old’s name was mentioned on the Stick To Football podcast, and the situation hasn’t gotten any better for our number 14 in the meantime.

Barring a substantial injury crisis in the forward line (heaven forbid), it’s hard to see the Italian getting much of a look-in at Anfield any time soon, and it’s looking increasingly likely that he could be allowed to leave for his homeland in January.

It’d be a shame of his time with the Reds petered out to that extent, but Chiesa would depart as a genuine cult hero among Kopites for what he has contributed over the past two-and-a-bit years.

#2056. Serie A preview: AC Milan vs. Inter – Team news, opposition insight, stats and prediction

On Saturday night, AC Milan face Inter in a game that needs little to no introduction. It’s time for the Derby della Madonnina.

After their defeat in midweek, Milan must end October on a high note. It’s a game that could define their season – a daunting sentence to say only a few months into the campaign – such are the sides of the scale.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Ruben Amorim was happy to admit that his side needed to improve after the recent inconsistencies in his press conference on Friday night, and with two defeats in three games, he’s unfortunately right.

Game date: Saturday, October 31 Kick-off time: 20:45 (CET) Venue: San Siro Referee: Marco Guida (VAR: Mazzoleni)

As mentioned, this is a huge game for Milan, simply because of how they arrive at this game. Defeats to Bournemouth and Bologna in their last two midweek fixtures have had an impact on hopes for this season.

So, if they are to prove that they are ready to compete, they must show it against one of Europe’s best sides. Saying that, the Nerazzurri are not invincible and Amorim’s side can get the better of them at San Siro, but they will have to fight for 90 minutes.

Unfortunately, the Portuguese’s job is not made much easier, with several injuries still to contend with. Fikayo Tomori headed to the medical room this week, after suffering a torn muscle in his right thigh.

He joins Matteo Gabbia, Alexis Saelemaekers and Samuel Chukwueze, amongst others there. However, Amorim has been given the boost of three potential returns. Indeed, Adrien Rabiot, Mario Gila and Diego Moreira are all expected to be available in some capacity. To what extent, though, remained largely unknown for most of Friday.

Looking at the loss to Bologna, the injury issues had clearly had an impact on the team, as Ruben Amorim named a heavily rotated side, with only five starters on the pitch from the first minute. Though that may have been to combat Saturday’s game.

In the defence, there will be no changes to the core, as Mike Maignan starts in goal, with Koni De Winter and Strahinja Pavlovic ahead of him. However, both full-backs will be changed, with Gila returning to the starting XI, alongside Davide Bartesaghi.

Luka Modric also returns in a starting role alongside Rabiot, who will be entrusted with a starting role after recovering. Then, it will be a full-strength attack, or close to it.

Omari Hutchinson keeps his spot, with the Englishman showing signs of consistency, whilst Moreira also returns from injury. After signing his renewal – which could be worth €10 million per season – Christian Pulisic will start behind Goncalo Ramos.

Updated with the latest Gazzetta dello Sport prediction below

Predicted Milan XI (4-3-3): Maignan; Gila, De Winter, Pavlovic, Diawara; Musah, Modric, Rabiot; Moreira, Ramos, Pulisic.

Predicted bench: Torriani, Bouyer, Estupinan, Vladimirov, M. Cissé, Vos, Perera, Bartesaghi, F. Terracciano, Musah, Jashari, Comotto, Ossola, Menon, Camarda, Cisse.

Injuries & suspensions: Chukwueze, Gabbia, Tomori, Saelemaekers, P. Terracciano.

In the summer, Inter oversaw a period of change, with several of the old guard departing. Davide Frattesi headed to Lazio on loan, Denzel Dumfries left to Real Madrid for €20 million, whilst Stefan de Vrij, Yann Sommer, Francesco Acerbi and Matteo Darmian all departed as free agents.

Changes would also come with the incoming mercato, though, as the Nerazzurri spent more than €100m. Djed Spence, Manuel Akanji, John Stones and Curtis Jones arrived from the Premier League, for a combined fee of €75m. Then, Aleksandar Stankovic returned from Club Brugge, with Ivan Provedel also making the switch from Lazio.

Whether those names have been an upgrade so far is difficult to tell, but it’s certainly been an introduction of a new wave of talent.

After dominating in Serie A last season, Inter have started the season in similar fashion, only dropping points to Roma so far. However, they’ve been something of comeback kings, regularly finding an escape when behind.

In fact, in their last three Serie A games, they’ve conceded the first goal – including the midweek disallowed goal against Venezia – yet they’ve always ended up with three points. The inevitability from recent seasons hasn’t disappeared.

What makes this potentially more frustrating is that they’re also struggling with injuries, but still getting results. Without Lautaro Martinez, Stones, Jones and Benjamin Pavard, a drop-off would’ve been understandable, but it hasn’t happened.

After their win in midweek, considering their schedule has also been rough, Chivu rotated slightly. So, there will be a few changes made this weekend to rotate back to their full-strength XI.

In the backline, Manuel Akanji will return to the centre of the back three, replacing Carlos Augusto. Whilst Alessandro Bastoni and Yann Bisseck will start either side of the Swiss defender. Of course, Ivan Provedel remains between the sticks.

Across the midfield, changes will be slightly more common. Federico Dimarco and Andy Diouf will remain on the flanks, whilst Piotr Zielinski retains his starting spot. Though Nicolo Barella and Hakan Calhanoglu both return to the starting XI.

Marcus Thuram will be given a starting role, hoping to continue his fine form this season, but Ange-Yoan Bonny will return to the bench. Pio Esposito will take his place instead.

Predicted Inter XI (3-5-2): Provedel; Bisseck, Akanji, Bastoni; Diouf, Barella, Calhanoglu, Zielinski, Dimarco; Thuram, Esposito

Predicted bench: Martinez, Di Gennaro, Augusto, Jakirovic, Bovio, Mkhitaryan, Lavelli, Mosconi, Spence, Bonny, Stankovic, Sucic.

Injuries & suspensions: Pavard, Jones, Stones, Martinez, Henrique.

Saturday’s contest will be the 243rd meeting between the two sides and, after the horrific period of defeats between 2023 and 2024, Inter sit the happier of the two, with 88 wins to the Rossoneri’s 83.

Saying that, it’s the Diavolo who are currently enjoying a better time of things, having avoided defeat in their last seven meetings. Last season, this record was made even better, with a double taking place, thanks to two 1-0 victories, with goals from Christian Pulisic and Pervis Estupinan.

➤ AC Milan have won three of their last four Serie A matches against Inter (D1), as many as they had in their previous 16 meetings (D4 L9). The Rossoneri have won their last two matches and have not won three consecutive matches against the Nerazzurri since a run of four under Carlo Ancelotti between 2002 and 2004.

➤ Inter have won more matches (70) and scored more goals (260) against Milan than any other team in Serie A history. However, the Nerazzurri have also conceded 236 goals against the Rossoneri, fewer than those conceded against Roma (237) and Juventus (270); with 496 goals in total, the Milan derby could become the third match in the competition’s history to reach the 500-goal mark, after Inter-Roma (544) and Inter-Fiorentina (502).

➤ Milan have collected 18 points from their first nine games of this Serie A season, the same amount they achieved at the same point last season; in five of their previous six seasons in the top flight, the Rossoneri have collected at least 21 points after the first 10 games, with the sole exception of 2024/25 (17).

Nobody realistically expected Liverpool to challenge for the title at the start of the season, so it wouldn’t be a failure if the Reds aren’t in contention for the trophy by the time April rolls around.

The objective for this campaign was to finish closer to the summit and show discernible improvement on a wretched 2025/26, and recent performances suggest that Iraola is capable of delivering in that regard.

His team are currently on course to end the season with 63 points (just three more than last term), but if they improve on a home record of just one win from five league games so far, they should be able to nudge that projected total into the 70s.

Liverpool competed admirably with Arsenal and Man City (up until the harsh red card for Ryan Gravenberch) but weren’t as clinical as the top two in those games. With more ruthlessness in attack, the Reds seem capable of at least closing that gap.

Van Dijk is correct – the goal for this season isn’t to compete for the title, but to qualify for the Champions League with relative comfort and lay the foundations for further improvement in 2027/28.

There’s still plenty of room for improvement, but at least there are signs of this campaign being much more convincing than 2025/26 had been.

#2050. Palladino takes advantage of a vacuum: Tactical analysis of AC Milan 2-4 Bologna

AC Milan suffered their first Serie A defeat of the season as Ruben Amorim’s decision to rotate with Saturday’s derby in mind backfired.

Samuel Mbangula became only the second player to score a hat-trick against Milan at San Siro (in the three-points-per-win era), joining the legendary Gabriel Batistuta in the record books. It overshadowed Alphadjo Cisse’s brace, which had put the Rossoneri ahead in the first half.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

How did Raffaele Palladino’s Rossoblu manage to score three without response in the second half and win 4-2? Rohit Rajeev has the tactical breakdown.

Milan lined up in a 4-2-3-1 formation, with Estupiñán at left-back, Tomori at right-back and Jashari and Musah forming the double pivot.

Regardless of the personnel or positional rotations, the underlying attacking structure remained the same: a 3-2-5 shape, with Milan maintaining five players in the attacking line.

The biggest flaw in Milan’s structure was the lack of central occupation. In their attempt to overload the wider areas and stretch the opposition, they often left the middle of the pitch vacant.

This exposed the central channels, making it easier for the opposition to exploit the spaces between Milan’s midfield and defensive lines.

Bologna’s first goal came from the intense counter-pressing often associated with Palladino’s teams. Milan initially dealt well with a Bologna counter-attack, with Estupiñán finding Musah.

However, Musah failed to escape the subsequent pressure, losing possession under Bologna’s aggressive counter-press. Bologna quickly transitioned forward, releasing Zortea to deliver a cross, while Mbangula was left unmarked between Koni De Winter and Tomori to finish.

Milan’s first goal was a direct result of the coordinated pressing between Hutchinson and Cissé. Hutchinson applied physical pressure on Theate, while Cissé blocked his forward passing option.

With Theate’s body orientation restricting his choices, he was forced to attempt a switch of play, which Milan intercepted to capitalise on the turnover.

Hutchinson played a crucial role in Milan’s second goal. By dragging Theate out of position, he created a sizeable space behind the Bologna defender, which De Winter exploited with a long pass into the vacated channel.

Cissé’s movement was equally intelligent. He initially stayed in an offside position, keeping himself out of the defenders’ immediate focus.

However, as Tomori delivered the cross, Cissé timed his movement to get back onside and attack the ball. A striker-like movement that demonstrated excellent positional awareness and timing.

Bologna’s second goal came from a wide free-kick situation, with Milan opting to defend using a high defensive line.

Miranda delivered an in-swinging ball towards the six-yard box, where a lack of communication between Bartesaghi and Diawara proved costly. Their misunderstanding allowed Bologna to capitalise and find the equaliser.

The central vacuum in Milan’s structure, mentioned earlier, came back to haunt them for Bologna’s third goal.

Bologna initially progressed through the middle, but Milan managed to deal with the immediate danger. However, when Bologna recycled possession, Cissé failed to track Miranda’s movement, allowing him the time and space to deliver a cross that Mbangula converted.

Bologna’s fourth goal originated from a Milan turnover on the left flank. Diawara initially won possession back, but Camarda was immediately surrounded by four Bologna players.

Unable to escape the pressure, Camarda surrendered possession, allowing Bologna to regain the ball and launch another attack.

With Amorim deploying a high defensive line, winning individual duels in the wide areas becomes crucial. Any failure to do so leaves Milan vulnerable to quick combinations and runs in behind.

Bologna repeatedly exploited this weakness by creating 2v1 situations against De Winter, while Musah was positioned too far away to provide adequate defensive support.

Bologna clearly had the edge in physical intensity, covering 2km more than Milan over the course of the game.

Milan’s players, meanwhile, appeared to be struggling with fatigue, which was reflected in their reduced intensity and ability to sustain defensive pressure.

"He surprised a lot of people last season with what he did for Sunderland, he set the standard, lead his teammates, and inspired some very impressive displays.

"He did a brilliant job, and maybe he was playing above himself, but this season he hasn't quite been at that same level.

"Sunderland haven't been at that level anywhere on the pitch this season, it's not just Xhaka, a lot of these players aren't reaching the heights that they were reaching before.

"So they need to get back to where they were last season, and that has to be led by Granit Xhaka, because he was instrumental in everything they did last season.

"He has got to do that again, he's got to step up and show how it's done, he needs to inspire his teammates and drag them up because he needs to show that leadership.

"That's the only way Sunderland can get out of this situation, their best players need to step up and be counted."

As previously mentioned, Xhaka's performances are far from the only concern at Sunderland at the moment, with multiple issues contributing to their poor performances.
